On motion of Hon. T. W. Crothers (Minister of Labour) the House went into Committee on the following proposed resolution, Mr. Blondin in the Chair:
Resolved, that whereas the use of white phosphorus in the manufacture of matches constitutes a menace to the health of match factory employees, and is also attended with danger to the community at large, it is expedient to provide that the manufacture, importation and sale of matches made with white phosphorus be prohibited, and in connection therewith that the Commissioner of Patents be empowered on petition to fix terms for the use of any process patented at the time of the passing of this Act for the manufacture of matches without white phosphorus, and to provide for the inspection of any place where it is suspected that matches made with white phosphorus may be found; and to examine anv receptacle or place in which it is suspected that such matches may be; and to authorize the Governor in Council to make such orders and regulations as may be necessary; and to fix penalties for infractions of the Act.

The. Bill to be founded on this resolution provides for the prohibition of the manufacture, sale and importation of matches made with white phosphorus. White phosphorus is a deadly poisonous substance and the object of the Bill is to protect against that poison those who are engaged in the manufacture of matches and also the homes of the people generally throughout the country. There have been cases where children, attracted

by the bright tips of the matches that are in every household, have been poisoned by putting the poisonous substance into their mouths. The white phosphorus match also provides a very convenient and inexpensive poison for criminal purposes. There have been cases of that kind. Hon. gentlemen will remember the case in Prince Edward Island, only a few years ago, where a mother poisoned three of her children by shaving off the ends of these matches and feeding the poisonous substance to the children. It is not necessary in the manufacture of matches to use white phosphorus. There are other substances that aTe being used extensively.
More expensive?

At a very trifling additional expense. My hon. friend will perhaps be aware of the fact that in 1906 the Government of Switzerland called, together a convention for the purpose of discussing this and other questions, and many of the leading countries in Europe at that time adhered to the convention, undertaking to prohibit the manufacture, sale and importation of matches made with white phosphorus.
England at that time did not adhere to the convention, because she had adopted some years previously very stringent regulations which it had been hoped would do away with the danger in connection with the manufacture of matches. But she discovered a year or two afterwards that even these most stringent regulations were not *sufficient to prevent the injuries that were being caused, and in 1908 she adhered to the convention also. In the United States, a similar law has been passed, not directly prohibiting the manufacture, sale, and importation of matches-because a question arose as to the jurisdiction of the Congress to do so-'but in a roundabout way, by putting a heavy tax upon such matches, they have secured the desired result. The law prohibiting the use of white phosphorus in the manufacture of matches has been adopted in nearly every civilized country.
I am satisfied, from information I have, that the use of other substances does not add materially to the cost of producing matches. A few years ago, the main substance used as a substitute for white phosphorus, and which is still used as such, was sesquisulphide of phosphorus. At that time the Diamond Match Company of the United States had a patent in 'Canada which would prevent any one from using sesquisulphide of phosphorus except by license
from the patent commissioner, but since then the patent in Canada has lapsed, so that any one is free to use it now. I am also told that the provision we make in this Bill will not incur any material additional expense for altering the machinery. The principal factory of Canada, operated in Hull, is now making large quantities of matches with this substance.
I have personally interviewed three out of the four factories doing business in Canada, and none of them have any objection to this Bill. A year or two ago I was led to believe that by installing a ventilating apparatus the danger might be removed from the factories, but I am now satisfied that such is not the case.
Very recently several cases of disease from the use of white phosphorus have appeared. I had an opportunity of seeing some of these patients myself in the hospital. The disease resulting from the use of white phosphorus is a very terrible one, and it is more widespread than is generally supposed.
Mr. GEORGE E. FOSTER: From the use of that substance in manufacturing?

Yes. The fumes of
this poisonous substance are inhaled by those who are working in the factory, and these fumes are absorbed by the teeth and gums, especially if the teeth are decayed, and an inflammation sets in which destroys the teeth and works its way into the jawbone, especially of the lower jaw. The only remedy is to take the jawbone out. The disease sometimes extends to the upper jaw as well. These are the direct results, but there are indirect results, as naturally might be supposed. A man or woman working in these factories and inhaling the poisonous substance is injured indirectly by the hrwer vitality and lessened strength to resist the ordinary diseases that attack humanity. It has a tendency to decompose and make brittle the bones throughout the whole system. There have been cases where the larger bones of the extremities break very easily as a result of the inhaling of this poisonous substance. It seems to me that there ought to be no hesitation in passing this measure. No one will be injured by prohibiting the use of this substance; the extra cost is only a few cents on 70,000 matches.

Does this Bill follow
the Bill introduced in this House in 1911?

It us substantially the same. The Bill to which the hon. gentle-

man refers did not contain any prohibition against the sale of matches made with white phosphorus, but it did prohibit their manufacture and importation. I think it well to include in this Bill the sale, because a large quantity of these matches might be imported before the date fixed for the coming into effect of the Act, and unless there was a prohibition the sale might continue for six months or a year afterwards. I have fixed the date for the coming into force of this Act in 1916.
I was waited upon by a large delegation from the Royal Society-the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) was one of the gentlemen present-and they thought that the provisions of the Bill should not be brought into force before the first day of January, 1916, so as to give the different factories, and those who have large quantities of these matches on hand, an opportunity to get rid of them before that.
Did my hon. friend accept the suggestion that the Bill should not come into force until 1916?
Yes. The Bill that was introduced into this House two or three years ago post-dated the date of its coming into operation by about two years.

Yes, but that was two years ago, and the public have had two years to be poisoned since then. The Minister of Labour is quite right, I think, in the details he has given as to the effect of this poisonous substance. I have heard of several instances, especially of young girls wrorking in the factory in Hull, whose health has been irretrievably destroyed by the use in the factory of that substance, not only because the fumes are inhaled, but because their hands, being covered with this substance, they may imprudently put them to their mouths. I do not see any reason why the public should be exposed for a further period of two years to the evil consequences which the hon. gentleman has described; I think the Bill should come into operation at a much earlier date.

As the minister has
stated, I accompanied the delegation which was appointed by the Royal Society of Canada at its last annual meeting to urge upon the Government the necessity of passing this legislation,- When the delegation was before the minister, at the end of last fall, one of the most noted Canadian chemists and scientists read a memorandum wThich was agreed to by all the other scientists present. There is no doubt as 
to the need for such legislation. I entirely concur in the remarks made by the minister, but I agree with the leader of the Opposition that this is either a poison or not a poison, and if it is a poison we should safeguard the public at a much earlier date than that proposed in the Bill.

My hon. friend will
remember that the opinion expressed by the gentlemen who waited on me, was that it should not come into force until 1916, There is some force, I admit, in what my right hon. friend says-considerable force. Personally, I should have no objection to letting the Act come into force at an earlier date. Perhaps we could discuss that on the second reading, and I should be wdlling to consider any suggestion on that line.

As the manufacturers of matches acknowledge, according to the Minister of Labour, that the use of this material is very dangerous, and say that they are willing to quit it, one would think they ought almost to stop this manufacture without being compelled to do so by law. They have had warning for at least three years that such legislation. was pending, and if they had been wise, particularly under all the circumstances and considering the effect of this manufacture, they would have been prepared for this legislation to come into effect almost immediately after its enactment. They are not in the same position as if legislation had not been foreshadowed several years ago when Parliament almost pronounced upon the matter finally. I think it would be of interest, if the minister, wdien he is advancing this Bill through its other stages, were to give us some information as to the manufacture of matches in Canada, the places where that manufacture is carried on and the quantity produced, together with the amount of white phosphorus used.
I have all that here, and will give it later. -

Can the minister tell us how many manufactories will necessarily be closed if this Bill passes? I remember that when the matter was discussed on a previous occasion in this House, it was stated that there was a factory in Halifax using this material and I think there was another in New Brunswick. I do not know whether the minister has considered the point that this match manufactured with white phosphorus is known in the Maritime provinces as ' the sailor's match.'

Sailors and fishermen light their pipes with these matches, which are much better for that purpose than other matches. The ordinary match in use throughout the United States and Canada goes out very readily in a gale of wind, while this hard match, which, I understand, is manufactured with white phosphorus, is found useful to this class of men who live in the open and use matches in windy weather.
I mention this matter in case it may not have been called to the minister's attention.

I understand that no factories will be closed by the passing of this Bill. I have had the advantage of consultation with the head of the firm in Halifax referred to by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sinclair), and he told me that he also was in communication with, or had some connection with, the factory in Hampton, N.B. He told me that they were quite willing that this Act should pass, although he explained that their factory had been in operation for seventy years, and they had never known a case of white phosphorus poisoning there. I do not know that my attention has ever been called to a case in either of these factories. Of course, we know that the large factory is in Hull, and all the cases to which my attention has been called have arisen in that factory. The gentleman in Halifax, Mr. Corbett, I think, said that they would be quite satisfied if a reasonable length of time were given them before the Bill was brought into force, and he thought that two years would be a reasonable time. The only other factory, I believe, is in Deser-onto. None of them will be closed by reason of this Bill.
Resolution reported and concurred in.
Mr. CROTHERS thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 103, to prohibit the manufacture and importation of matches made with white phosphorus.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

On motion of Hon. 1. D. HAZEN (Minister of Marine and Fisheries) the House went into Committee to consider the following resolution, Mr. Blondin in the Chair:
Resolved, that it is expedient to repeal the Acts relating to the harbour of North Sydney, in the province of Nova Scotia, and transfer the property, rights and assets now held by the
harbour commissioners to His Majesty, and that His Majesty do assume all the obligations and liabilities of the said commissioners.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The object of this measure, as appears on the face of it, is to abolish the Board of Harbour Commissioners of North Sydney. For a number of years past representations have been made to the Government and to my department by persons interested in the welfare of shipping at this port that no useful purpose was being served by the commission and that it should be abolished and the harbour managed, as many other harbours in this country are by the department, through a harbour-master. These representations have pointed out, and have established, I think, beyond question, that the imposition by this commission of tolls on shipping entering the harbour of North Sydney was in the nature of a discrimination against this harbour from which no corresponding or adequate advantage was derived. Under the terms of the Act which it is proposed to repeal, the commissioners are authorized to collect dues from all registered vessels of forty tons and upwards that enter the harbour, and these dues are at the rate of one cent per ton; and in the case of large vessels this would amount to a very substantial item in the course of a season. The total revenues collected in 1912 by the commissioners were $3,917.60. Of this amount, $1,637 was paid as salaries to commissioners and harbour-masters, and practically the whole of the balance was expended on repairs to the break-water at what is known as the North bar. In addition to the representations made by individuals separately, a numerously signed petition from the citizens of North Sydney was received in favour of abolishing this harbour commission, and the board of trade of North Sydney has had the matter under consideration and has forwarded a resolution in favour of such abolition.
I understand that North Sydney is situated on the north side of the harbour of the same name and that it is the principal shipping point of the Nova Scotia Steel and Coal Company. The port of Sydney, on the other hand, is on the south side of the harbour and is the principal shipping point of the Dominion Iron and Steel Company. Ships from Sydney are exempt from such dues as are imposed by the commissioners in North Sydney on shipping entering that port, and it is contended, and I think with some degree of force and cogency, that the shipping at both ports should be on an equal footing

and that it is practically a discrimination against the port of North Sydney that an extra tax should be placed on shipping there over that placed on shipping at the port of Sydney. It is reported by officials of my department that the liabilities of the Harbour Commission at the present time amount to about $800, and against that there are assets of considerable value, consisting of what is . known as the ballast ground property, and the right of way to same, the Bertram property, and the breakwater property at the north bar. Under this legislation the liabilities of the Harbour Commission are assumed by and the assets of the Harbour Commission are vested in the Government. The management of the harbour will be assumed by the Marine and Fisheries Department under the Harbour Commissioners Act. A harbour commissioner will be appointed, and will be paid, as harbour commissioners are, a commission on the dues that are collected, to a certain specified amount. On the second reading of the Bill it is my intention to move an additional clause providing that the Act shall come into force on January 1, 1915. There are certain matters that have to be settled in connection with the taking over of the property, and it is considered that it will be 'better to have the Act come into force on January 1, 1915, than to have it come into force immediately upon the passing of the Bill.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. D. McKENZIE (North Cape Breton):
speechtext:
I have listened with some
interest to what has been said by the hon. minister with reference to the resolution before the committee. I am quite familiar with the complaint that the collection of dues by the harbour commissioners of North Sydney has been a discrimination against the harbour. The Board of Harbour Commissioners is an old institution ; I think it has been in existence for the last thirty years or thereabouts. There are officers who, I suppose, will regard it as a hardship if these dues are wiped out of existence by legislation based on this resolution. However, if it is in the best interests of the harbour that these dues should be removed, I certainly should not stand in the way of any action in that regard. Are the dues out of which the harbour-master is to be paid akin to those that the hon. minister proposes to abolish? If they will be as large as the dues now collected, of course the object 
of this Bill will be defeated. I would suggest to the hon. minister that there should be no dues at all. If he is to make the port of North Sydney a free port, it should he absolutely free. I think the harbour-master of the port receives only about $600 or $700 under the commission. That is a very small amount, and it is hardly worth while keeping in operation the machinery necessary for the collecting of dues df the object is only to provide for the salary of the harbour-master. I am sure that I would be entirely in favour of anything that is in the interests of the port.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
With the passage of this proposed legislation the tolls of one cent a ton applicable to vessels of imore than forty tons will disappear altogether, and that is the principal source of revenue. In every harbour certain dues, sick mariners' dues and things of that sort, Which do not amount to very much, have to be looked after, and under the Harbour Commissioners Act the commissioners can only be paid a certain percentage of the dues collected, up to a maximum amount to be specified. Speaking from recollection, I think that under the Harbour Commissioners Act no harbour commissioner can receive more than $600. On the second reading of the Bill I will produce a statement of the dues that are no.w collected at Sydney. It is proposed that North Sydney, so far as dues are concerned, shall be placed upon the same footing as the port of Sydney.
Resolution reported and concurred in.
Mr. HAZEN thereupon moved for leave to introduce iBil'l No. 104, respecting the harbour of North Sydney in Nova Scotia.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

On motion of Hon. J. D. Hazen (Minister of Marine and Fisheries) the House went into committee to consider the following proposed resolution, Mr. IJlondin in the Chair:
Resolved, That it is expedient to consolidate and amend the Canada Shipping Act and the Acts in amendment thereof, and various laws relating to Merchant Shipping.
Resolution reported and concurred in.
Mr. HAZEN thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 105, to consolidate and amend the Canada Shipping Act.

He said: This Bill, as its title indicates, is one to consolidate and amend 4 p.m. the Canada Shipping Act. Such a consolidation has been d's-cussed, I understand, by the Department of Marine and Fisheries for some years past. It has been felt to be very desirable that there should be a consolidation of the different Acts that have reference to the Canada Shipping Act and also certain amendments of a more or less important character. The Bill is a lengthy one, and there may be very considerable difference of opinion about some of its clauses among those who are interested in shipping. It is therefore my intention, on the second reading of the Bill, to move that it be referred to the Select Standing Committee on Marine and* Fisheries so that there may be, perhaps, a more careful consideration of the provisions of the Bill in that committee than is usually possible in a Committee of the Whole House. I have given instructions that a considerable number of copies of this Bill should be printed so that they may be circulated among those interested in shipping in Canada, in order that we may find out what objections they may have to its different provisions, and so that they * may have an opportunity, if they desire to do so, of appearing before the Marine and Fisheries Committee and placing before that committee the views which they entertain regarding any provi-' sions of the proposed measure. It may be, considering the length of the Bill and the very many sections that will have to be considered-although a great many of them are largely sections as they are at present in the Canada Shipping Act-that it will be impossible to get the Bill through the House at the present session. In that case, the matter can stand over until the following session. In the meantime the different interests in Canada that are affected by its provisions will have an opportunity of fully discussing them, and at the next session of Parliament we may be in a better position thoroughly to consider the Bill. I have thought it desirable, as the Bill is one of very considerable importance to large interests in this country, that I should place on ' Hansard ' at the outset a resume or summary of what the Bill contains and, if the House will pardon me, I shall take the opportunity of doing that now. It may have the effect of expediting the consideration of the matter and placing in more succinct form than otherwise could be done before the members of this House and 98	.
before the shipping interests of Canada, the different provisions of the Bill and what it is sought to achieve by it.
In order that the necessity for a complete revision of the Canada Shipping Act may be apparent, the history of shipping legislation in Great Britain and Canada should be considered.
The earliest imperial legislation which need be mentioned is the Merchant Shipping Act of 1854, which was a consolidation and revision of all the previous legislation upon the subject. During the following forty years numerous amendments were made to the Act, and in 1894 it was again revised, and, although ftumerous amending Acts have since been passed, notably one of great importance in 1906, it is the Act of 1894 which is the constitutional source of legislation relating to merchant shipping throughout the empire.
This Act, like its predecessor of 1854, performs two functions.
Upon many important subjects, such as, for instance, the registration of ships, it legislates for British ships all over the world.
On other equally important matters, it deals only with ships registered in the United Kingdom, leaving the other parts of the empire to legislate with regard to these matters as they deem best.
Even with regard to the first class of subjects, however, some latitude was left to the colonial legislatures.
Thus, in the Act of 1854, by section 574, a colonial legislature was given power by Act or Ordinance, confirmed by Her Majesty in Council, to repeal wholly or in part the provisions of the Act relating to ships registered in that possession. A similar provision is found in section 735 of the Act of 1894.
In 1873, two important Acts relating to shipping were passed in Canada. These were chapters 128 and 129 of 1873, entituled respectively, ' An Act relating to shipping, and for the registration, inspection and classification thereof,' and ' An Act respecting the shipping of seamen.' These Acts are printed at the beginning of the statutes of 1874. By the terms of both these Acts, which were reserved for the signification of the Queen's pleasure thereon, and were thereafter duly confirmed by Her Majesty the provisions of the Imperial Act of 1854, so far as ineons!stent with the terms of those Acts, were repealed.
At the same session of 1873, a number of other Acts relating to shipping were passed by the Canadian legislature, as to which it

was not considered necessary to obtain confirmation by Her Majesty. All these Acts were from time to time amended, until the revision of the Canadian statutes in 1906, when all the Acts relating to shipping were collected into one Act which was called ' The Canada Shipping Act,' being chapter 113 of the Revised Statutes, 1906. In connection with this revision no attempt appears to have been made to redraft the Act, or to improve its arrangement or its phraseology. Since that revision further amending Acts have been passed, especially one in 1908, when an attempt was made to bring the Act in some particulars more up to date.
It will be seen, then, that the present Act is a conglomeration of a number of separate Acts, most of which were written while the Imperial Act of 1854 was still in force, and of a great number of amending Acts, all of which were designed to remedy some defect or defects which had revealed themselves in the practical working out of the Act, and that for forty years no effective attempt has been made to modernize the legislation upon this most important subject. The two Acts of 1873 already referred to, together with the Coasting Trade Act in 1870 and the Masters and Mates Act in 1871, are the only ones which have ever been confirmed in the United Kingdom, and there are many provisions in the Canadian legislation which, if tested in the courts, might be held to be ultra vires of the Canadian Parliament for want of confirmation.
It has been found, too, that many of the provisions are obscure and of doubtful meaning, and many new provisions are required by the ofiicers of the department charged with the enforcement of the shipping laws in Canada. So many changes and improvements have taken place during the past forty years in the construction and operation of ships that they in themselves require that the language of the Act should be modernized.
It is proposed, therefore, to pass a new Act, based upon the latest imperial legislation, and so drawn that .it will be acceptable to and be confirmed by the imperial authorities-an Act dignified, modern and consistent-adjectives none of which could with any regard for truth be applied to the existing legislation.
Many of the changes which have been made in the present revision are changes of phraseology only, designed to reproduce, wherever desirable, the exact language of the Imperial legislation, and thus to make available for the interpretation of the Act the vast number of authorities which have

accumulated in the United Kingdom in connection with merchant shipping legislation during the past sixty years. Apart from these changes of phraseology, some substantive alterations in the law of shipping in Canada are proposed. These will be dealt with in connection with the various parts into which the Act has been divided.
Part 1-Registration and Classification of Ships.
Very few structural changes have been made in this part. Provisions have been inserted giving the minister power to appoint surveyors of ships. This has been found to be necessary especially in connection with the accommodation on board ships for seamen and apprentices. The Board of Trade in the United Kingdom have power to appoint, and have appointed, surveyors. The power of appointment in Canada has heretofore been vested in the Governor in Council.
Another change proposed is with regard to the registering of the names of managing owners. In the existing Act, provision is made for registering changes of managing owners, but there is no obligation to register the name of the original managing owner.
A section providing for a master submitting himself for examination after a shipping casualty has happened, has been transferred to another part of the Act, which seemed a more appropriate place for-it.
Provisions have been made by which vessels exempt from registration shall annually take out a license, and have the license number and the port at which they are licensed painted on their bows and sterns. This has been done because it has been found in practice very difficult to identify small vessels, such as motor boats, which have violated the law in any particular, or to identify the owners of such vessels.
A section has been inserted defining the proper national colours for Canadian ships.
There were in this part a number of sections providing for mortgages on ships in course of construction. These have been found to be of no particular value, and have therefore been omitted.
Part 2- Masters and Mates.
A serious condition of affairs has arisen in the past few years with regard to sailing ships owned in the Maritime provinces. The owners of many of these ships found

the requirements as to the certificates oi masters and mates so onerous and so difficult, if not impossible, of fulfilment, that tjbey withdrew their vessels from their Canadian registers and had them registered in Barbados, where the restrictions as to certificated officers are practically nil.
There were really two difficulties, each affecting a different class of owners. One related more particularly to masters, the other had more special reference to mates. The first difficulty arose out of the definition of a coasting voyage, which, for the purposes of this discussion, may be considered only from the standpoint of its southern limits on the Atlantic, which was the fifth parallel of north latitude. This would permit a master with a coasting certificate to take a vessel as far south as Berbice, in British Guiana. It happens, however, that cargoes frequently offer for Brazil ports, but a Canadian registered vessel could not clear from a Canadian port for Brazil unless her master held a full Board of Trade certificate, or its equivalent. Competent and desirable men holding such certificates cannot be procured for comparatively small sailing craft, or if so, only at a prohibitive price. By registering these ships at Barbados, however, they need not have a certificated master at all, and, as the Canadian law stands, they could not be refused a clearance from Canadian ports.
The second difficulty arose because vessels of over four hundred tons could not engage in coasting voyages, "or trade on the inland waters of Canada, unless they carried a certificated mate. Many of our sailing ships are over four hundred tons, and it has been found impossible to procure certificated mates to sail in such ships.
The imperial Act allows vessels (not carrying passengers) to trade between United Kingdom ports and ports on the continent of Europe between Brest and the river Elbe without any certificated officers whatever, and in the United States no certificated officers are required for sailing ships under seven hundred tons.
It was thought that the restrictions imposed in this respect upon our freightcarrying sailing ships were too great, and that an effort should be made, by making those restrictions more reasonable, to induce the owners of those ships which had been registered in Barbados to transfer them back to their Canadian registers. To this end, two amendments to the existing legislation are proposed. First, to deal with the case of ships desiring to trade with Brazil it was felt that the limits of a 98i
coasting voyage should not be extended further south because some criticism has already been made by the Board of Trade of the present extensive limits of that class of voyage. It is proposed, therefore, to have a new class of certificates to be called ' limited foreign-going ' which will enable an officer to go in a vessel to the West Indies, Bermuda and Bahama Islands, or to any port on the continent of America, or on any adjacent island. The holders of the present coasting certificates will be enabled to qualify for the new certificates by passing an examination upon the practical use of the chronometer and sextant, with which they are all now necessarily familiar. Second, to meet the views of the owners of the larger sailing ships, it is proposed that the limit of tonnage necessitating the employment of certificated mates be raised to five hundred tons. It is understood that some important amendments of the Imperial Shipping Act may be expected in the near future, as a result of the conference recently held in London, and it is likely that this legislation will define for the empire the distinction between ocean going voyages and those not ocean-going. This may seriously affect so-called coasting voyages in connection with ships leaving Canadian ports, and will, almost certainly, involve some readjustment of the law in Canada. It is, however, impossible, with the information which we have at hand, to forecast the form which the imperial legislation will take. It may be, however, that before the revision of the Canada Shipping Act becomes law, the imperial legislation will have taken definite shape. In that case, the proposed Canadian legislation can be modified accordingly.
Before leaving this important question, it should be pointed out that it affects, not only the certificates of masters and mates, but also the certificates of engineers, and the quantity and quality of life-saving equipments, &c., to be carried by the various classes of ships. Oceangoing steamships will be obliged to carry a much more extensive equipment for lifesaving, fire-extinguishing, &c., than those which are not ocean-going, by whatever name they may be called.
Parts 3 and 4-Seamen, and Shipping of Seamen on Inland Waters.
It has been found possible and desirable to combine these two parts into one, and thus save a great deal of needless repetition. Many amendments affecting the matters dealt with by these parts have been made

in England, which have not been incorporated into the Canadian legislation. This has necessitated the complete re-writing of the part. No substantial change has, however, been made in the policy of the legislation.
Some changes are proposed with regard to agreements with crew, or ships' articles, as they are more generally called, by which the limit of tonnage of home-trade ships required to have agreements with the crew, is reduced from eighty to fifty tons, registered tonnage. With regard to homS-trade ships of between fifty and eighty tons, the agreement may be signed either before a shipping master or other respectable witness. In all other cases, the agreement must be signed before a shipping master. Similar provisions have been made with regard to the discharge of seamen. The provisions with regard to seamen's advance notes and the allotment by them of their wages have been considerably amplified to conform to the practice in the United Kingdom. The provisions in the Canada Shipping Act in respect to property of deceased seamen, destitute seamen, leaving seamen abroad, and distressed seamen, have been brought into line with the most recent legislation in the United Kingdom, and the provisions of the Act have been very materially extended for that purpose. In other important respects the Bill proposes that the Canadian legislation should be assimilated to that of the United Kingdom. This has been done without materially affecting the substance of the existing legislation.
Bart 4-Sick and Distressed Mariners.
This part was found to be in such an unsatisfactory condition that it was considered advisable to have it completely rewritten. The sequence of the provisions has been re-arranged to bring them into a more natural order. No substantial change has been made in the substance of the provisions of this department, but many obscurities have been cleared up, and the part, which was most unsatisfactory in form, is now clear, logical and consistent.
Part 5-Pilotage.
The principal, indeed the only important change proposed in this part is one by which the Minister of Marine and Fisheries constitutes the pilotage authority for Canada.
The intention is to have pilotage administered as one system throughout Canada and, while it is proposed to have local pilotage authorities, they will be more _ 
under the control of the department than heretofore, and it will be possible to have a more uniform administration of the law than has hitherto obtained. This change is proposed in accordance with the recommendation of the Pilotage Commission.
As the establishment of one pilotage authority for Canada will automatically abolish all the existing local pilotage authorities, all references to local pilotage authorities have been eliminated.
A provision has been inserted by which pilots will cease to hold licenses after they attain the age of seventy years. A new class of ships to be exempted from the provisions of this part is proposed. On the Atlantic coast, steamships employed in voyages between Canadian ports and the port of New York or other United States ports north of New York, have been exempt. It was thought that a similar exemption should be given to steamships trading between British Columbia ports and the port of San Francisco or other United States ports north of San Francisco.
Part 6-Steamship Inspection, Examination and Licensing of Engineers.
This part has been re-arranged and largely re-written and amplified, but no important structural changes are proposed. The number of motor boats on our inland and coast waters during the past few years has so enormously increased, and the provisions with regard to their inspection and regulation were so inadequate that it was considered advisable to give to the department ample powers in those respects for the future. The regulation of the speed at which they may be diven in waters of restricted area, of the number of passengers which they may carry, and a number of equally important matters are beyond the powers of the department under the existing legislation. These matters it is proposed to put under the control of the department for the future. During, and previous to, the present session, the department has been receiving representations from different individuals and people interested in maritime matters in regard to the necessity of providing that these motor boats shall be equipped with mufflers to deaden the sound which they make as they are being driven through the water. Under this provision the department will be able to make regulations dealing with that question which, judging from the reports we have received, has become one of undoubted importance.
Vessels such as steam dredges, floating

elevators, etc., are to be brought under the operation of the Act as regards regulations governing equipment for life saving, fire extinguishing, etc. The application of the law as regards this type of vessel has generally been made clearer.
It has been considered desirable that power should be given to the minister to make regulations upon a number of important matters under this part, which in the United Kingdom, are regulated by the Board of Trade. These are all technical matters relating to boilers, machinery, equipment, strength of materials and structures, methods of construction, inspection and other matters, the details of which it would be impossible to incorporate in the Act.
The procedure upon inspection of hulls or machinery has been very much improved and brought into line with that in force in the United Kingdom.
Some changes, more of expression than of substance, have been made in the provision relating to the employment of engineers on the various classes of ships. In making these changes, the practice in the United Kingdom has been taken as a guide.
It is proposed to eliminate a number of provisions of the existing Act which deal with matters which from their nature would seem to be more properly dealt with by regulation, either because they are not of sufficient importance, or are too much matters of detail to appear in the Act. Other sections which hafe outlived their usefulness have been eliminated.
Part 7-Safety.
The practical value of this part has been immensely increased, and, dealing as it does with very important matters relative to the lives and health of passengers and crews, a great deal of careful attention was given to it in the revision. The principal matters dealt with are:	(a) Unseaworthy
ships; (b) dangerous goods; (c) deck loads; (d) grain cargoes.
No substantial change in the law, except in one important particular, has been made in connection with unseaworthy ships, but the provisions for enabling ships suspected of being unsafe to be detained for survey and amelioration have been made much more effective, and have been brought into line with those in the United Kingdom and the other principal possessions of the Crown. The exception referred to. is with regard to the damages and expenses to which a ship-owner might be exposed if his ship were detained, and it proved that
the suspicions as to her unseaworthy condition were not well founded. Under the existing legislation the ship-owner would have no redress except against the complainant who might be a man of straw. It is proposed that the minister, that is to say, the Government, shall be liable to the ship-owner for those damages and expenses, with a right of action over against the complainant, if any, and the right, as at present, of exacting from a complainant security for these damages and expenses before taking action upon the complaint. In the United Kingdom and Australia and New Zealand the Governments have assumed liability for these damages and expenses. It is thought that Canada should do as much as they under similar conditions. Another reason exists, however, for the proposed change. It has been found that existing legislation is almost a dead letter, because the department cannot act without first receiving a complaint in writing. This leaves the most important cases of all unprovided for, namely, those in which a ship is suspected of being unseaworthy on the eve of putting to sea, because in such cases there would usually be too little time for a written complaint to reach the minister and for an order for detention of the ship to be procured. It is proposed, therefore, in line with the legislation in the United Kingdom, Australia and New Zealand, that the proper officials of the department should, be empowered to act immediately that there, is good ground to suspect that a ship is about to put to sea in an unseaworthy condition, and upon their own initiative if a complant is not received. If this proposal becomes law it is only just that the Government should be responsible if it proves that the detention in any case was after all unjustified.
With regard to dangerous goods a more general definition has been adopted and it is proposed that power shall be vested in the minister to determine from time to time by regulation what goods are to be considered dangerous and to provide for the packing, and stowage and handling of the. various kinds of dangerous goods. These are matters of detail which cannot be properly dealt with in the body of the Act.
No changes of any importance have been made with regard to deck-loads. The provisions on that subject of the Merchants' Shipping Act of 1906 were added to the Canadian Act by an amending Act in 1908, and those provisions with slight verbal changes have been repeated in this revision.
Some slight verbal alterations have been

made in respect to grain cargoes. The only addition which is proposed gives power to the minister to make regulations upon the subject.
Three sections have been transferred to this part from Part 8 of the existing Act and a new section has been prepared and added to them in connection with the appointment and duties of Inspectors of Ships' tackle, of whom several have already been appointed.
Part 8-Wreck and Salvage.
The only substantial changes which are proposed in this part are those which are rendered necessary by the ' Maritime Conventions Act, 1914 ' now before Parliament. It is assumed that that Act can be disposed of, and it is, therefore, proposed to incorporate in the general Act in the appropriate places all the provisions of the ' Maritime Conventions Act, 1914/ and to repeal the last mentioned Act when the general Act comes into effect.
Part 9-(Special Shipping Inquiries and Courts.
This part, which with one relating to wreck and salvage forms one part in the existing Act, has been almost entirely re-written and brought more closely into line with the provisions of the Imperial Act, but the changes are almost entirely verbal. It has been thought wise, however, to give power to appoint legal assessors as well as those of nautical, engineering or other special skill or knowledge. In the United Kingdom, courts of inquiry into shipping casualties always have at least one legal member. In Canada the Court is usually composed of the Wreck Commissioner, assisted by two nautical assessors, none of whom have any legal training. In special cases where important questions as to the advisability of evidence or of substantive law might arise, the court would be much stronger if it could call to its aid a good legal practitioner to advise the court in any such matters. In ordinary cases the services of a legal assessor would neither be required, nor procured. The provisions relating to the appointment of the person to hold formal investigations have been enlarged so that the minister will not be restricted to the judges and officers mentioned in the existing Act, but may appoint for that purpose any person whatever, having practical or technical knowledge.
It has often happened that an investigation could not be promptly held after a shipping casualty, even when the Wreck Commissioner was in the neighbourhood,

and witnesses have had to be detained, often at considerable expense and inconvenience, because the commissioner had not actually received his commission from the department to hold that particular inquiry. It is proposed that no formal appointment or commission shall in future be necessary, but that the commissioner, or other officer, judge or person selected, may act upon the receipt of a letter or telegram from the minister directing him to hold the investigation.
Part 10-Lighthouses, Buoys and Beacons, and Sable Island.
The only substantial change proposed in this Part is to vest the power of appointment of all lightkeepers in the minister, Under the existing Act, the minister can appoint keepers whose salaries do not exceed two hundred dollars per year. All other keepers must be appointed by Order in Council. This is felt to be too unimportant a matter to be dealt with by Council.
Part 11-Public Harbours and Harbourmasters.
The only new matter dealt with by the revision of this Part relates to the salaries of harbour-masters. Some difficulties have been experienced in the past in dealing with this matter under somewhat equivocal language in the existing Act. This matter has now been put beyond question, and no further difficulty is anticipated in this respect.
Part 12-Port Wardens.
The changes proposed are merely verbal ones.
Part 13-Navigation of Canadian Waters.
The only changes proposed in this Part, other than verbal ones, are those necessary to give effect to the provisions of the Maritime Conventions Act, 1914.
Part 14-Coasting Trade of Canada.
No changes, except verbal ones, are proposed in this Part.
Part 15-Delivery of Goods.
This is an entirely new Part, so far as Canadian legislation is concerned. It has been adapted from Part 7 of the Imperial Act of 1894. It is intended to provide for a difficulty which not infrequently occurs in connection with the delivery of goods at their destination when the consignee for any reason refuses or neglects to pay the freight or take delivery of the goods. The shipowner is then placed in a quandary. It is true that he has a lien on the

goods for the freight, but it is a possessory lien only. He loses it if he in any way parts with the exclusive possession of the goods, as he would do, for instance, if he were to land them and store them in any ordinary warehouse. In that case, the warehouseman would acquire a lien for his charges, which would not only have priority over the shipowner's lien 'but would actually destroy it, because he would have surrendered the possession to another person entitled to a possessory lien. It is true he can retain the goods on board the ship, but, in that case, he cannot charge demurrage for the ship. His only alternative is to store them in a warehouse which is ufider the exclusive control of himself or his agent. Such warehouses are rarely available, so the quandary is a genuine one. The object of Part 15 is to provide a means by which the shipowner may store the goods in any ordinary warehouse, or other place of deposit of goods, and, by giving certain notices, and taking certain other steps, preserve his lien against the goods. Provision is also made for the necessary customs entries being made, for sale of the goods if the lien is not discharged, for payment of the shipowner's lien and the charges of the warehouseman by the owner of the goods, and generally for the effective working out of the Tights of the various parties, without ousting the jurisdiction of the courts to determine any matters of difference between the parties. Legislation of this nature is a practical need in Canada, and should have been on our statute books years ago.
Part 16-Liability of Carriers by Water.
This part has been expanded to include the provisions of the Water Carriage of Goods Act, 1910, and an amending Act of 1911.
Part 17-Legal Proceedings.
This is a new part modelled upon one in the Imperial Act. The existing Act, made up as it is of a number of separate Acts thrown together more or less haphazard, contained no consistent scheme for putting the numerous penal provisions into force. Some parts lacked all provisions of that character, others had some, none had sufficient. The provisions relating to procedure have been taken out of the various parts and put into this special part together with such other provisions as were necessary to round out the matter. In addition some very necessary provisions which do not appear in the existing Act have
been added. Among these are provisions governing the taking and using of depositions of witnesses who are by reason of illness, absence from Canada, or other good clause, unable to appear at a trial, and others dealing with the jurisdiction of courts, damage occasioned by foreign ships, detention of ships, proof and service of documents and application of penalties.
Part 18-Supplemental.
In this part are collected provisions with regards to the following, among other subjects:	documents and forms; powers for
enforcing compliance with Act; Orders in Council, rules and regulations; transmission and publication of documents; definitions; repeal; commencement of Act. Of these 'definitions' alone require any special mention. In Hie existing Act each part had its own definitions which were often inconsistent with definitions in another part or parts. The definitions of the same word were not identical throughout the parts, and many essential definitions were missing. Thus, for example, steamship, steamer and steamboat were differently defined in different parts, but no two of those words were defined in the same part. Yet it was by no means rare to find several of those words used in the same part, apparently with the same intended meaning. To rectify this condition of affairs, the word ' steamship ' was adopted as the synonym to be used throughout the new Act; that woTd was defined; and the words ' steamboat ' and * steamer ' no longer appear in the Act, except, perhaps, by inadvertence. The principle has been adopted of having one set of definitions for the whole Act, and these have been compiled with great care. It is true that some special definitions still appear in a few of the parts, but these have been retained because they appear in that way in the Imperial Act, and it was thought better to preserve as far as possible in all cases the exact form of the parent legislation.
Some few general observations may be permitted. The work of revision, clerical and otherwise, has been collossal. Out of 970 sections in the existing Act, hardly one but has had at least some verbal changes made in it, and most of them have been so altered in form as to be almost unrecognizable. As a matter of fact, the whole Act has been practically re-written, and many sections have undergone that process repeatedly before they assumed their final shape. Two parts

which were obsolete or useless have been omitted, and two new parts, those relating to delivery of goods and legal proceedings, have been inserted. Another part, that dealing with wreck and salvage and investigations into shipping casualties, has been subdivided into two parts. The result is that the proposed Act is longer by one part than the existing Act, but, on the other hand, as the Tesult of careful pruning away of useless matter which has taken place, no less than 226 sections have either disappeared or have been combined with other sections. We have 744 sections in the proposed Act, as against 970 in the existing one.
It should be mentioned that the work of revision has been performed under very high pressure. The work was not begun until late in July, 1913, so that less than eight months have been devoted to it. It was thought desirable that the proposed legislation should be introduced into this House at an early date in the present session. In order to make that possible the work, of revision has proceeded with unusual speed. Partly as a result of this, imperfections will undoubtedly appear. They will be, I am sure, the imperfections of speed, not of carelessness.
The proposed Act is not a mere consolidation; it is intended to be a complete revision of the legislation upon this most important subject, with a view to providing for Canada a code for merchant shipping which will be worthy to take a dignified position alongside the legislation upon the same subject in the motherland and in the other great possessions of the Crown. We have been too long labouring under the disadvantages of a code which was crude, obsolete, obscure, and unworthy of a great nation. It is high time that we took our place in this respect with the other great maritime powers of the world.
I feel I should apologize to the House for taking up so much of its time, but I thought time might he saved in the future were I to place a complete summary of the legislation upon 'Hansard', so that it can be studied by hon. members of the House and others interested in the shipping interests of the country.

nrnister rightly, he said that captains holding coasting certificates have to submit themselves to an examination before being permitted to sail further south than 5 degrees north latitude.

The only examination which a man having a coasting certificate will have to pass will be an examination on the use of the sextant and certain other instruments which that captain undoubtedly knows how to use at the present time.

It will be very inconvenient for captains now engaged in the service to submit themselves for examination. I would submit to the minister the importance of dealing with the question at the present session. I understood from the hint he threw out that he scarcely expects this Bill to become law this session, and as the matter is an urgent one, I hope he will consider the advisability of facilitating the passing of a Bill that I introduced very early in the present session. This case illustrates how difficult it is for a private member to get his views before the House. I introduced my Bill on the 21st of January, only a few days after the opening of the session. I have been in my place every day since, yet I have not had an opportunity to move the second reading of that Bill nor to explain its purport to the House. But the minister is familiar with the matter, and he admitted in the House recently its great importance. I would urge upon him the desirability of dealing with it prior to . this Bill because, if it could be dealt with at the present session, it would be of great advantage to the shipping interests throughout the country.

On the motion of Hon. George E. Foster for Committee of Supply:

Mr. Speaker, it is my intention, before closing my remarks, to move an amendment to this motion, which amendment I will read now. It is as follows:
That ' all the words after the word ' that ' be struck out and the following substituted therefor:

In the opinion of this House the time has arrived when, in the interests of the farmers, and consequently in the interests of the whole of Canada, the duties on agricultural implements should be forthwith removed.
I desire to address myself to this question in no controversial manner, but rather, if possible, to speak of it from such viewpoint that I may appeal to both sides of the House, and to offer remarks which may commend themselves to hon. gentlemen whether they sit upon your right or on your left. The question is one of too great importance, and the principle involved is too fundamental, to justify either myself or any other hon. gentleman on either side of the House making it a mere political question for party purposes; for it involves the problem of supplying those engaged in the great agricultural industry of this country with what is. in reality a very important part of their raw material. I think it goes without saying that the people who use agricultural implements, namely, our farming classes, are the foundation of our country, the basis of the success and prosperity of the Dominion, and that everything that contributes to their success contributes to the success of our whole nation. There are many other industries in Canada but none that can commence to compare with the agricultural industry in point of importance. If you were to take away from our economic activity the interest of the farmer, you would have no Canada left. In our own province of Saskatchewan, or in the province of Manitoba, or in the province of Alberta, take away the grain grower, and you have no city of Winnipeg, no Regina, Moosejaw, Edmonton, Calgary, Saskatoon or Prince Albert. For, if you remove the tiller of the soil, the grain grower, you remove the man who keeps every person in the town in employment and in supply of the necessaries of life. Take the city of Moosejaw, for instance: if there were no grain growers in the district, there would be no bankers in Moosejaw, no lawyers, no clergymen, no schoolteachers, no milliners, no merchants. So I might take each town in the prairie country and show you that the whole system of our towns depends on the prosperity of our agricultural classes. And just as it is true in that absolute way that unless we have an agricultural class we shall have no city class, it is true to a proportionate degree that to the extent to which we encourage and make prosperous our agricultural classes we encourage and make prosperous our city and town classes.
Legislation enacted in this House will be, in the last resort, wise legislation which o-oes to the very root of our national prosperity, namely, the success of our agricultural classes. Therefore, I make no apology for taking the time necessary to bring before hon. gentlemen the necessity of bringing relief to our agricultural classes in the manner of which I have spoken.
The motion of which I have spoken, and with the moving of which I shall close my remarks, makes the assertion that because it will be for the benefit of the farming class, therefore the step I advocate will be for the success of the whole nation. That,
I think, is clear upon the face of it. As my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark) yesterday so well said, it is surely false economy to believe that you are going to make a successful nation on the basis of milking the industries which are natural to our country, industries which succeed here on their merits and stand on their own feet, and give to other industries that are artificial and not able to stand alone.
I desire to express the view-and I wish I had words that would express as forcibly as I feel the importance of what I am going to say-that the Dominion of Canada to-day owes more than it has ever realized to the people who started the farms of this country from the Atlantic to the Pacific.
I speak, of course, as a western man, but I trust that this motion will commend itself to those interested in the agricultural industry in the East, and to people interested in the prosperity of Canada everywhere. We do not give sufficient recognition to people who have taken the land which had remained unproductive since it left the Creator's hands and turned it into a source of national wealth. Whether in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Quebec, Ontario or the West, the man who has gone upon the land which for ages has lain without being the source of any benefit or wealth, and as a pioneer has turned it to a source of wealth, is the man to whom the greatest credit is due, he is the man to whom in this House the greatest consideration should be shown.
My riding is an immense one. At one time I represented a district embracing 400 miles along the line of the Canadian Pacific railway, from forty miles east of Regina to eighty miles west of Medicine Hat, and from the international boundary line to the top of Township 34, over 200 miles. My riding is not now so large, but is still a vast one. 1 have gone through that

riding at different times; I have seen ttie homesteaders, the first men to go on	the land. I have seen their
humble circumstances, their poverty, if you will; I have seen the hard row they have had to hoe, and I have thought that notwithstanding their modesty, they, after all, are the men who make the Dominion of Canada, and not the millionaires who sit in the clubs in the cities of Montreal and Toronto. When you come to analyse the success of the Canadian nation, you are brought face to face with the fact that the men who have built up Toronto and Montreal are these same men who have taken homesteads; men. who had, perhaps, pledged their credit for a pair of oxen and have gone out upon the lonely prairies to till the virgin soil. For that reason I feel that I may with confidence appeal not only to hon. gentlemen on this side, but to members on both sides of the House, because there is not in the House to-day an hon. gentleman who does not realize that he and his constituents-nay, all of us, as Canadians-have a greater Canada to-day because of the development that has taken place in the prairie provinces. I ask for the co-operation of my hon. friends on the other side, who represent the tillers of the soil in the prairie prov,incus. I believe they must realize the truth of what I have said in regard to the privation which the farmers have had to undergo, and will agree that they should give the most favourable consideration and support to any course of action which will result in the introduction of legislation beneficial to their constituents. Although, as I have said, I am going to try to keep away from the controversial side of the matter, I may point out that hon. gentlemen opposite are, at this juncture, in a position to do more than we on this side of the House are able to do. Such gentlemen as the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Schaffner), the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bradbury), the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen), the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. McKay), are able to do more than we are, because they have the ear of the Government. May I remind them that the constituents whom they represent feel the pressure of present conditions upon them, and require relief in one form or another.
If hon. gentlemen analyse the vote of the people in 1911, they will see that the farmers of Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba are not satisfied with the present condition of affairs. Let us analyse the vote, just for a 
moment. I wish to refer first to the election returns for the county of the hon. member for Souris. That hon. gentleman was just as good a man in 1911 as he was in 1908; personally, a perfectly good man in every way, I am confident. He supported a policy that denied to tire farmers the measure of relief that was offered to them from the pressure under which they were existing and are now struggling. What was the result? His constituents sent to Ottawa a message, just as definite as if they had elected a Liberal candidate, that they were not satisfied with the existing condition of affairs. The majority which my hon. friend had in Souris was reduced from 880 in 1908 to 61 in 1911, the latter being but one-fifteenth of the majority he had before. I am not reflecting on my hon. friend; I simply use that fact to convince him and hon. gentlemen of this House that the people of Souris sent a message to the Parliament of Canada that they desired some measure of relief from the pressure of conditions under which they were struggling. Take the constituency of the hon. Minister of the Interior (Mr. Eoelie). In 1908 he had a majority of 560 in 1911 it was reduced to 126. His majority in 1908 was four and a half times that amount. Take the case of the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Sharpe). His majority was reduced from 105 to 20. The majority of Mr. Staples, who is not now in the House, was reduced from 576 to 161.
What about the last majority in Macdonald?

I am glad my hon.
friend asked me that question; it serves to show that although it is my desire to avoid the controversial aspect of this question, he is more inclined to make some petty political capital out of it than he is to serve the farmers of Lisgar. Unless my hon. friend wants to have his majority reduced not to one-fiftli of what it was before but made five times as large again on the Liberal side, he had better take to heart the advice I give him, leave party politics alone in respect of these important matters, and attend to the farmers of Lisgar county, or they will attend to him at the next election.
The hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen) is a shining exception to tlie rule. He was the same hon. gentleman in 1911 as he was in 1908-just as strong, just as able on his feet or off his feet. He increased his majority, multiplying it by three. And why? Because he

was the man who got up in this House and said that he was in favour of the reduction of the duties on agricultural implements. In the election of 1911 my hon. friend was everywhere in the Prairie provinces regarded as the man who, if his party came into power, would be the apostle of free agricultural implements for the farmers. This exception to the rule convinces me of the truth of the principle which I am endeavouring to establish as underlying the election of 1911. The people gave the hon. member for Portage la Prairie the increased majority that they denied to his colleagues because they thought they were voting for a man who, in power or out of power, would advocate what he preached while in opposition. But to their sorrow he has been more than 2 years with his party in power and done nothing.
Let us take Alberta. In 1908, Mr. Herron, of the riding of McLeod, had a majority of 273; the hon. member who now represents that riding reversed Mr. Herron's majority, making it a Liberal majority of 819. Mr. McGrath, in Medicine Hat, had a majority in 1908 of 300; the present member for Medicine Hat defeated Mr. McGrath and had a majority of about 1,500. So 1 could go over the different constituencies, I could take this one and that one m Alberta, I could take my own in which, from one thousand, the majority was increased to twenty-three hundred because the farmers of the district of Moosejaw wished to send to Ottawa the message that they desired some release from the pressure and strain under which they were struggling in their agricultural operations.

How do they propose
to pay their share of the national expenditure?

They propose paying
this share, but not, as they are doing now, much more than that.

and then pay nothing.

My hon. friend had
better not get into a discussion of protection. I repeat that the people of these provinces have, as emphatically as it is possible for them to do so, sent
5 p.m. their message that they wish relief in some form or other. I do not care greatly whether we get it in the open market offered in the south or in the lowered duties on goods purchased, I would like both forms of relief, but relief we wish and ought to have. I might
say that we must have it if we are going to continue to assist in building up the prosperity of Canada as we have done in the past.
The question will be asked, and I am sure my hon. friends opposite will raise it, as to whether the Liberal party is altogether in an ideal position on this question of the tariff on agricultural implements, or the tariff as a whole. There is no doubt that that is a question that will be raised, for it is raised on every occasion that hon. gentlemen opposite seek to defend the present conduct of the affairs of the Dominion of Canada. In order to anticipate the objection or the twitting that might be offered to me on that score, I may say that, in my humble opinion, neither party in Canada has gone as far towards a lower tariff as I would have liked them to go. When I differ from my party I am not afraid to say so; but I am just as clear on this as that I am standing on my feet, that as between the two parties, for the man who has the interest of his constituents at heart, if they are farmers in the West, there can be no debate or hesitation as to which party he ought to support. I quite understand a person saying that neither party goes far enough, but I cannot understand a man representing the farmer on the prairie saying that he thinks the Conservative party is the better of the two from the viewpoint of his constituents. One party goes a certain way, a long way towards that relief, and the other goes the other way, being the protectionist party. Sc, 1 say, as between the two, I can have no hesitation in standing before my constituents or in this House and saying that, much as I regret that the former Government did not go further than it did, yet, as between the two parties, there can be no question as to which I deem it my duty to support in the interests of my constituents. As long ago as 1908 I uttered words in this House which I have recalled before, and which I shall recall again. On the 1st of June, 1908, as will be found on ' Hansard,' page 9,514, of that day, I uttered the following words, and they were my view then and they are my view to-day. Speaking with reference to the duty on lumber, 1 said:
I deliberately state that protection is the mother of trusts and combines. Tariffs breed trusts and if there is one thing in which there should be no trust, that thing is lumber. For my part, I am against protection from start to finish, protection is to me an abomination. I support the Liberal party because of the two parties it is the one that favours the lower duties. But if a strong party de-

cidedly devoted to free trade were to arise, I would be a supporter of that party, regarding its tariff policy. In this House, as representing my constituents, I believe I serve them best by supporting the party that goes the furthest in granting a low tariff.
That was my view then and it is my view now. I say also for the Liberal party that not only did they effect very substantial reductions in the tariff while they were in office, against the bitterest opposition of the hon. gentlemen now in power, but they went down to their defeat because they were in favour of a further reduction in the tariff and offering us the American markets, and thus aroused the enmity and hostility of the trusts and mergers and combines in this country. The whole Liberal party is very often twitted on its conduct on the question of the tariff. Sometimes it is said that the platform of 1893 committed the Liberal party to free trade. I do not need to read that platform to you; you know very well, and hon. gentlemen of this House know it did not. The policy of the Liberal party, as laid down then, was that free trade as they have it in England should be the goal towards which the Liberal party should look in the Dominion of Canada. These are the words spoken by the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier):
I propose to you from this day forward, that it would be the goal to which we aspire.
I propose to you from this day, although we cannot adopt the policy itself, to adopt the principle which regulates it; that is to say, that though it should be your misfortune for many years to come to raise a revenue by customs duties, those duties should be levied only so far as is necessary to carry on the business of the Government.
And I think there is nothing inconsistent as between that policy as laid down there and the policy as it was carried out by the Liberal Government while in power. I will make the statement that I would not be so foolish as to advocate that free trade should be introduced to-morrow or forthwith. I do not know how many hundreds of millions are invested in manufactures in this country. A man would be foolish to say that all of that should be jeopardized and every whit of tariff removed.
The Liberal policy is a sane one: we are not iconoclasts. I am dealing with the duty on agricultural implements, and before I conclude I shall try to show that the abolition of the duty on agricultural implements is such a move as even protectionists should agree to, because the time has arrived when they

need no more protection but are able to stand absolutely on their own feet.

The same position that I take now, namely, serving my constituents to the best of my ability.

I say that, on the

That this House, regarding the operation of the present tariff as unsatisfactory, is of opinion that this country requires a declared policy of such adequate protection to its labour, agricultural products, manufactures and industries as will at all times, secure the Canadian market for Canadians.
