In the last fiscal year drawbacks amounted to $306,168, which was either a present to the manufacturer or a bonus to the foreign purchaser at our expense.
There is another reason, and it follows from the one I have just given, why the manufacturer of agricultural implements stands on a different footing from other manufacturers, and it is this: he can go into the world's markets and successfully compete against the manufacturers of other countries. If he can do that successfully in other countries, why cannot he do it in Canada? If the farmers of Great Britain, having money to spend, find that the Massey-Harris Company, the International Harvester Company or any other company manufacturing binders in Canada, can sell to them cheaper than the American manufacturer, why cannot our Canadian manufacturers, with all their loyalty, sell to their fellow-Canadians as cheaply as the foreign manufacturer can? They desire to build up Canada for the Canadians. Why do they then give this great privilege to Frenchmen, to Germans, even to Russians and to Australians? Why do they not give to their fellow-Canadians, since they want to help Canada, the same terms that they give to the purchasers of their manufactured articles away across the seas? They can compete in the world's markets with the manufacturers of the United States or of any other part of the world. I do not wish to refer to a past debate, but the hon. member for East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) last night made the observation that the manufacturers of agricultural implements in Canada could undersell, and compete successfully with, the manufacturers of agricultural implements in Germany, Australia or any other country, and could meet the exported article from any other country in fair competition. Even the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. White) seemed to say the same thing. He even went farther in his argument the Minister of Finance went so far as to say that he was going to take into consideration the question of putting a duty oil pig iron, as his supporters asked him to do, and he added: If I do that I will have to take into the consideration the question of increasing the duty on agricultural implements. When I heard him say that about in-
creasing the duty on implements, 1 thought it was high time that we had a motion to the effect of that which I am going to place in your hands, Mr. Speaker.
Let me observe further that the manufacturers of agricultural implements can go, not only into the world's markets, but right into the United States and compete successfully. I see my hon. friend from Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) here. He will bear me out when I say that the manufacturers of agricultural implements in Canada can pay the United States tariff, pay the freight and sell substantially all their goods in the United States.
What is the United States tariff on implements?
I am not positive as to the present, but at the time my figures have reference to, it was 15 per cent on ploughs. If I am wrong, will my hon. friend .correct me?
Not just now.

Not just now. I will live in hopes that he never will. I know I am right. The company of which I have the data is the Cockshutt Plow Company. My hon. friend from Brantford will believe me when I say that I do not bring it up because his name is connected with it, but it is because I have had access to the information on that point. The Cockshutt Plow Company, of Brantford, makes an eight furrow gang plough which at the time my figures were compiled-and as far as I know at the present time-sold at Brantford for $600, at Winnipeg for $680, and at most points in Saskatchewan for $705 cash. This same infant industry in Brantford, which requires 17J per cent protection before it is able to supply the people of Canada, is able to go into the United States, pay a duty of either 13 or 15 per cent, as it was at the time my figures were compiled, and sell this plough at Peoria, Illinois, for $525 and at Minneapolis for $502.
At what time were the hon. gentleman's figures compiled?

Since the present Government came in.
' Mr. MEIGHEN: Since the present Government in the United States or this Government came in?

No, this present Government. These figures which I am giving were given previously to this House in

the debate either in January, 1912, or December, 1911. If there is any difference in the American tariff now, it makes no difference to my argument. The cost of manufacturing has not at all increased, and if the Coelcslmtt Plow Company was able to do it under these circumstances it answers the purpose of my argument just the same. The same plough that sold at Brantford for $600 sold in Minneapolis for $502 after paying a duty of fifteen per cent besides the freight. Could anything more be wanted to substantiate my statement that this industry at least needs no more protection? If my hon. friend from Portage la Prairie, in raising this question, wishes to make the point that ploughs are now admitted free into the United States, it does not change the correctness of the argument I am making from these figures. They were then able to sell at a lower figure in the United States and pay the duty. If they are able to compete with the American manufacturer in the United 'States after paying the duty, surely, they are able to compete with the American manufacturer in Saskatchewan without paying the duty. If they can do that then my motion should be accepted by the hon. members of this House and by the hon. member for Brantford amongst them.
My hon. friend from Humboldt (Air. Neely), in the same debate, read in this House two letters which had been received by a certain gentleman who had written to the representative of the Cockshutt Plow-Company in Saskatoon and the representative of the same company in the United States and the figure given for an 8-gang plough at Saskatoon was $705 cash and the figure given for that plough at Minne-appolis was $541.20. This infant industry, the Cockshutt Plow Company, that needs protection from this Government, went away to the markets of the south of us and showed that they could compete, without any bounty or duty, with the American manufacturer right at home, while at the same time declaring that they cannot stand fair competition here in Canada. I could go over all the different implements in the same way. If I am not mistaken the southern boundary of the constituency of my hon. friend from Souris (Mr. Schaffner) is the same as the international boundary line. You can get agricultural implements on the one side and on the other and invariably they are' about twenty per cent dearer on the Canadian side than on the American side.
No, no.

My hon. friend says,
' No, no.' After the investigation which I have made I am convinced that the figures which I have here will bear out what I have said, and I do not wish to make any statement that is not correct. Let us take, for example, the figures given by my hon. friend from Regina (Mr. Martin) on December 28, 1911, page 474 of 'Hansard' and I would add that these figures have never been contradicted nor questioned by any hon. gentleman in this House, and several Conservative members spoke in opposition to Mr. Martin's speech but did not question the correctness of his figures; therefore I take it that they are correct. My hon. friend from Regina made this statement:
I have here figures obtained from implement men, and no doubt they are correct, and they show that in southern Saskatchewan the farmer has to pay $90 for a wagon which in Montana or Minnesota he can buy for $S0; that the farmer in southern Saskatchewan pays for 5 feet mowers $57 which are bought by the farmer in the northern states for $47.50 each. These figures also show that binders cost the southern Saskatchewan farmer from $150 to $160 each. I am told that last year they sold in Regina from $180, and the same mower can be bought for $140 in the northern states, then the Saskatchewan farmer has to pay $85 for a gang plough which can be bought for $70 across the line, and $57 for a hay-fork which his neighbour in the northern states can purchase at from $28 to $35. How is that explained? Is it fair that the southern Saskatchewan farmer should pay from 10 per cent to 20 per cent more for what he needs than does his brother farmer to the south of the line, just for the benefit of affording protection to the Canadian manufacturer.
These figures were given in the debate dealing expressly with this subject when hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House spoke and the figures given by my hon. friend from Regina were not in any way challenged either by the hon. member for Portage la Prairie, who has questioned the correctness of what I have just said, or by any other hon. member of this House. I therefore say that, in the absence of evidence to the contrary, there is a very substantial difference between the price which the American farmer has to pay in the West and that which the Canadian farmer has to pay. My hon. friend (Mr. Cockshutt) has an explanation of why he should be allowed to go into the American market and pay the duty, and yet, as a manufacturer, not be willing to stand open competition in the American markets, and this is the explanation he gave on December 5, 1911, page 810 of ' Hansard,':

Let me explain how these ploughs are used in order that thi3 House may understand thoroughly the position of this matter, because I charge here again that this is an endeavour to set the farmer of the west against the manufacturer, of the east. That is what the whole argument is designed to do and what has characterized the conduct of hon. gentlemen opposite. It is the desire of hon. gentlemen to set the farmer of the west against the manufacturer and the working man of the east. This plough that the hon. gentleman refers to will turn twenty-eight acres of new land per day. Let us see to what use this plough is put by the man who buys it. He takes a contract from his neighbour, who is not fortunate enough to have one of these ploughs, and he charges him from $4 to $4.50 per acre for turning the land. I have known of a case in the west where a man during a season has ploughed 30 acres per day at $4.25 an acre, making in all $138 per day. This is not bad business. We should consider that a very fair profit in the plough business. A man who would make that profit per day would probably have 100 days in the season in which he could do it, and after allowing $53 for labour and working expenses of the plough, he would have $75 as a profit on his day's work. If he had 100 days in a season this would give him $7,500 for the operation of his plough for a season of 100 days. So that I do not think the hon. gentleman has made out his case that this man is worthy of such an immense amount of sympathy.
This is the hon. member's reason for saying that it is right that the people of Saskatchewan should have to pay an inflated price for their ploughs. The statement happens to be very inaccurate, for unfortunately our farmers are not making the fortune my hon. friend imagines. But let that go, and let us investigate his argument. Let us see where that reasoning lands us. My hon. friend does not say that he needs protection; in fact, he cannot say that, when he pays his duty and goes into the United States and sells there. But he does say that the Canadian farmer m Saskatchewan is a money maker, and has the money, and therefore, by law, we should take it away from him. If the hon. member says anything at all, that is what he says. He says this man is making $138 a day, and therefore we should not take off this 20 per cent, but the manufacturers should continue getting nearly $200 more for their ploughs in Saskatchewan than they get in Minnesota, where they have to pay the duty, and this extra $200 taken by law from the farmer and given to my hon. friend's plow company. Did you ever hear such reasoning, Mr. Speaker ? If there is anything in that reasoning, it means that if a farmer in Saskatchewan happens to have $500 in the bank, and the Cockshutt Plow Company hears of it, and thinks he can live without it,

legislation would be justified which would take $300 from that farmer and give it to the Cockshutt Plow Company. The very fact that my hon. friend is driven to that argument, which is nothing but legalized robbery-and I make the statement without fear of contradiction-the very fact that my hon. friend is driven to say, that because the farmer in Saskatchewan makes money on his farm, therefore, it ought to be given to the manufacturing firm in Brantford, leads us to this: that we should pass legislation here to take the money away from the millionaires. If because a man makes money, and has lots of money to spare, we should pass an act which will take away from him $20,000 for each one of us to blow around the country as we think fit, that is the principle announced by the hon. member. If one is right the other is right, but of course both are absurd.
The very fact that my hon. friend from Brantford is driven to such an extremity to defend the protective system in connection with the products of the Cockshutt Plow Company, shows the weakness of the whole protective system.
As another reason why I contend that the Canadian manufacturers of agricultural implements should stand on their own bottom, I refer to the evidence taken before the Ways and Means Committee, which is the Tariff Committee, of the Congress, at Washington, in 1908-9. Here we have this witness stating that in the city of Hamilton they are able to manufacture practically as cheaply as they can in the United States, where their plant is an immense one of $120,000,000. There is the evidence right from the manufacturer who was at the head of the biggest concern in the United States, and possibly the biggest concern in Canada also, and he says, that the cost of manufacturing in the two countries is practically the same. If that is so, that the manufacturers in Canada can compete in the markets of the world-and I think I have shown they can-and that they can even compete in the American market after paying the duty; if Mr. Metcalfe, who knows the concerns in Canada .and in the United States, swears on his oath that it costs practically the same to manufacture in Hamilton as in Chicago, should we hesitate any longer? Should we not, on the contrary, come to the decision that the Canadian manufacturer of agricultural implements does not need any protection but can stand upon his own feet? The doctrine of protection-and I address myself of course to my hon. friends who are protectionists-if it is ever justifiable, is justifiable only when it is needful. With regard to the Cockshutt Plow Company we can find no justification for the seventeen and a half per cent duty, if it is not needed. My hon. friends will agree with me, I think, when I say that protection is wrong when it is not needed. For my own part I am against protection anyway, but we have protected interests in this country and you cannot be an iconoclast and smash everything. When the time comes when protection is not needed, it is robbery. If pro-99
tection is not needed to enable the manufacturer to carry on his business, and you continue that protection, you are taking money out of the hardworking farmers' pockets and giving it to other men who do not need it. I believe the time has come in Canada when these manufacturers do not need protection. There is a well-known manufacturing concern in Toronto, the Massey-Harris Company, a very honourable concern in every way, so far as I know. Do they need protection? Have they not been protected far more than they needed protection? If they were living just from hand to mouth and hanging on by their teeth, there might be some argument in favour of protecting them; but what do we find.? We find that they have money coming into their pockets by the millions of dollars to throw around the city of Toronto in philanthropy. I have nothing to say against philanthropy, but if the people of the prairie provinces want to build Massey halls, do not take the money from them to do so by legislation; let them give it freely by contribution, and not by the Massey-Harris route. I repeat, that it is not just to take this money from them by legislation, when the manufacturer does not need it.
There is a plant in New York state offered for sale; and this ' infant industry ' of the Massey-Harris Company, which must be supported with money taken out of the poor homesteaders can find $3,000,000 in cold cash to buy that plant, and they have doubled that plant since then. They do not need protection, and to continue protection to them is an outrage. I submit that the time has come when that protection should be removed. We have no money to contribute either as a present or as charity to the manufacturers.
The removal of protection on agricultural implements is, I think, in accord with the policy of hon. gentlemen opposite as well as in accord with our own policy. Because National Policy, so called, proposes to give protection only so long as it is needed, I do not think there is an exponent of the National Policy in this House who will disagree with me when I say that the underlying purpose of the National Policy when it was introduced was to nurture industries until they required no more nurturing, and then to leave them without protection. I would refer hon. gentlemen to quotations made by my hon. friend from Portage la * Prairie (Mr. Meighen) in 1911. The first is from the address of the present Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Foster) on



the 27th of March, 1894, and is reported at page 234 of ' Hansard ' of that year. The hon. gentleman was speaking with regard to the reduction he then made in the duty on agricultural implements when he reverted to the figure-20 per cent-that had prevailed under the Mackenzie Government:
After considering the matter in all its phases the Government has come to the conclusion to reduce these from 35 per cent to 20 per cent, a reduction of 15 per cent on the whole, and a reduction which it will tax the manufacturers of these implements to meet and keep the field in which their competition is at present even quite heavy, especially in the Northwest; but a reduction with which the Government believes that they can prosecute their industry, while, at the same time, it will have the effect of greatly cheapening one of the largest items of expenditure to which the farmer has been subjected, especially in grain-growing districts.
The late hon. member for South Lanark, the Hon. John Haggart, who was then a minister of the Crown and spoke with all
the responsibility of his position, speaking in the debate on the 28th of March, 1894, as reported at page 347 of f Hansard 5 said:
The policy of the Government has been to develop our industries and, so successful has that policy been, that the time is coming soon when not only can our manufacturers supply our own markets, but when they will be able to export to the markets of the world and to compete on fair and even terms with the manufacturers of any nation on the face of the globe. In Canada, nature has given us great facilities for manufactories. It is true in some places they have no coal, but nature provides another blessing in an immense water-powef*, which can be obtained at comparatively small cost. There is no reason why, by application of science to our natural resources, we should not be able to produce as good and as cheap articles as there are in the world, and to compete successfully in foreign markets as well. For the last fourteen years, protection in Canada has so developed our manufactories that the Government now think that a fair reduction in the tariff can be ventured on. They believe that . our people can compete with less protection than formerly, and to prove that, it can be pointed out that we are now sending agricultural implements to many portions of the world.
In view of these utterances as to the true purpose of the National Policy, I think the time has arrived when even the most devoted advocate and supporter of the so-called National Policy might now give his support to the motion which in a moment I shall place in your hands.
There is only one objection which may be raised to this motion that I wish to anticipate, and that is that it might embarras the Government and that it would be better < to deal with the matter at the time of the Budget. I do not take that view. I think

it right that the Government should know the opinion of this House. I appeal to the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Schaffner) and to all the gentlemen who come from the grain-growing parts of the West, as well as to the gentlemen who represent grain-growing counties in Quebec and in Ontario-and there are many of them. Now is the opportunity to leave party politics aside, now is the opportunity for hon. gentlemen on the other side to show to the Government they support that in their opinion the time has arrived for this change in the law. I say the matter will be quite in order. My hon. friend from Portage la Prairie moved a resolution, not on the occasion of the Budget, but as a private member's motion, some three years ago.

Not as an amendment
to Supply.

And perhaps not on
this day of the month; and there may have been other differences. But in effect the hon. gentleman sought the opinion of this House on the reduction of the tariff on agricultural implements in the same way as I now do. It is quite as much in order on t'his occasion to ask hon. members on both sides to signify by their votes at this moment what in their opinion the Government should receive as a message from those who represent rural constituencies in this House. I wish not to be sectional, and as the prosperity of Canada depends upon the prosperity of the lural districts, I believe that my motion is not provincial or sectional. In amendment to the motion that you do now leave the Chair, Mr. Speaker, for the House to go into Committee of Supply, I move, seconded by Mr. Thomson (Qu'Appelle):
That all the words after ' that ' be struck out, and the following substituted therefor:
In the opinion of this House, the time has arrived when, in the interests of the farmers, and consequently in the interests of the whole of Canada, the duties on agricultural implements should be forthwith removed.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. L. BORDEN (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friend from Moosejaw
(Mr. Knowles) began his speech with the declaration that he did not intend to approach the question in a controversial spirit. I am not quite sure that he succeeded in that as well as he intended. It is perfectly clear-and I wish to remind him of this in connection with his exhortations to hon. gentlemen on this side of the House-that when the late Administration was in power he succeeded in restraining

his emotions to the extent of not making any motion of this kind, and certainly not under such circumstances. He is aware, and all members of this Houses are aware, that declarations with regard to changes in the tariff are not made in advance of the Budget Speech of the Minister of Finance. Therefore, he understood perfectly well when he made this motion that no such declaration could be made at this time. Under these circumstances he has seen fit, although declaring that he does not approach the subject in a controversial spirit, to bring this subject forward in the shape of a motion of want of confidence against the Administration; and, of course, so far as we are concerned, there is only one answer to that-we cannot accept the motion proposed by the hon. gentleman, and if he does not withdraw his motion, it will have to receive the opinion of the House upon its merits as a motion of want of confidence in the Administration.
My hon. friend rather emphasized the spirit in which he approached the subject by not following the usual courtesy of giving us a copy of the motion before he made his speech, at least so far as I am aware no copy of the motion was furnished to us on this side of the House. For many years it has been customary, when a resolution of the kind was to be proposed, to furnish a copy the day before, or, at all events, several hours before the debate began. But, up to the time that the hon. gentleman began his speech, we were wholly unaware of the character of the motion which he proposed to present.

I sent a note the day before yesterday to the Minister of Finance, and told him as much as I knew about it then, informing him that on motion to go into Supply I would move an amendment dealing with the question of the reduction of duty on agricultural implements. It was only this morning that I finally made up the motion.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I understood that my hon. friend intended to make the motion yesterday. Of course, I at once accept his word that he did not know the precise form of the motion until this morning.

I knew what the motion was going to be, in effect, but I did not
know the exact wording of it. I do not think the Prime Minister knew that I had sent the Minister of Finance a note.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am not impugning in any way my hon. friend's assertion; I know 99i
that these motions require consideration, but it might, perhaps, have been better if the hon. gentleman had followed the usual custom in such cases, and have given us notice of his motion a little in advance.
My hon. friend has gone very fully into the question of the duty on agricultural implements. For the reason that this is not the time to discuss those duties, or to make any announcement with regard to them, I do not propose to follow him in the argument which he has made upon the subject. I shall content myself for the present with saying that the question of the duties upon agricultural implements, and the question of duties generally, has engaged and is engaging and will engage, from time to time, the attention of the Government, with a view to carrying out the policy upon which this Administration sought and obtained the mandate of the people of Canada. My hon. friend has spoken of the attitude of the Conservative party, and he has been good enough to quote a certain declaration of my own, made, I think, in 1903, and he has also alluded to the attitude of the leaders of his own party. So far as we aTe concerned, we have endeavoured to follow and be guided by that declaration of policy. The difference between the two parties, if a difference is to be sought, is that my hon. friends on the other side of the House have repeatedly declared themselves, not only upon the public platform but in solemn convention assembled-1 have the words under my hand at the present moment-to be absolutely opposed to the policy of protection, and to stand for free trade as it exists in England. Having made that declaration, and having sought the mandate of the people upon it, they came into power, and for fifteen years they practised a policy of protection. I have not failed to make my views known with regard to this question in every part of the country, even in parts of the country where the doctrine of an adequate protection to the industries of Canada might seem to be regarded with no great favour by the people. But I am bound to say that when I stood face to face with the strongest free-traders in the West and asked them whether they would desire the late Government or any Government to embark upon a policy which would mean the closing up of industries in Canada, involving tens of millions of capital and the employment of thousands of men, I found none who were prepared to urge the
That was only the beginning.

speechtext:
Of course the reduction
of duties upon agricultural implements, as well as upon other articles, does not always bring about the exact results expected. I believe that 25 years ago there were in -Canada not less than twenty or thirty plough companies manufacturing ploughs and competing with each other. I believe I have the figures somewhere, but they are not before me at the moment. The result of the reduction in duty from 35 per cent to 20 per cent was the elimination of nearly every one of these plough companies-the strong ones were able to stand-and it might be that the abolition of the duty, as now proposed by my hon. friend, would result in a still

further elimination. If there were absolute freedom of trade between the two countries, in this and in other respects-which, I know, my hon. friend from Red Deer would strongly advocate-it might be possible that the people of this country, delivered into the hands of an international trust in agricultural implements, might not find themselves very much better off in the end than they are now. I have never seen or heard any reason which would lead me to the conclusion that if there were absolute free trade between the two countries, the great trusts established in the United States would be any more merciful to or considerate of the interests of the people of Canada than they have been of the interests of the people of the United States. If any hon. gentleman on the other side believes that they would be more considerate of the people of this country in that regard I would like him to give me his reasons for reaching that conclusion. So far as trusts and combines among our own manufacturers are concerned, we have legislative powers in this country which ought to be capable of dealing with any evils that have arisen or might arise, but so far as international combines are concerned, there might be more difficulty in dealing with that question under conditions of free trade than there otherwise would be.
However, this is a question which should properly come under the consideration, in the first place, of the Minister of Finance and of the Government, and thereafter of the House when the proposals of the Minister of Finance, as outlined in his Budget Speech, are presented to the people of this country. In the meantime it is sufficient for me to say at the moment that, for the reasons indicated, I do not propose to embark at this stage upon an argument of the question either one way or the other, but to reserve the consideration of the whole question, so far as the Government is concerned, until the proposals of the Government with regard to the tariff, if any are to be announced, shall be placed before the House by the Minister of Finance in his Budget Speech.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

I gather from the remarks of the right hon. the Prime Minister, in discussing this

question, that he feels he has some grievance against the Opposition in regard to the time and manner of their bringing on this discussion. It seems to me his objections are not well founded. Rather than criticise us, I think the right hon. gentleman should be thankful that we have placed ourselves clearly on record; it strikes me it is a great advantage to my right hon. friend, as this question has to be dealt with by the Government. We know that he has sitting behind him a number of gentlemen who are not free traders, gentlemen who are looked upon by the country as high' protectionists, even if they themselves do not admit it. To these gentlemen the protective policy is a sacred thing which must not lbe tampered with whenever it can possibly be avoided. They do not wish to see the duties reduced or repealed except in very rare cases. The Government cannot expect the cordial support of these gentlemen, and if the Government wishes to bring in a measure to relieve the people of this country, and especially the farmers of the west, from the burdens of which they complain, it seems to me that they are placed in a very much stronger position by our action to-day, for now they know they can depend upon us to support any such measure. We are not only doing the Government a good turn, but we are giving our constituents, at least those of us who represent rural constituencies, a better chance of getting some relief from the present Government. So I have no hesitation in seconding the resolution of my hon. friend from Moosejaw (Mr. Knowles).
When the policy of protection was introduced into this country some thirty-five years ago, many reasons, or excuses if you like, were given for it. But I think the House will agree with me that the main reason given was that protection would encourage our infant industries; that it was necessary to prevent the ruin of our manufacturing industries through outside competition. That was the reason which led the people of Canada to accept protection, and but for that reason they never would have accepted it. It seems to me then that the questions we have to consider now are, first: Is the agricultural implement business of this country still in its infancy; and secondly, is it still in danger of ruin from outside competition? If these questions can be answered in the negative, we can fairly come to the conclusion that protection, so far as this industry is concerned, should be abolished. My hon. friend from
Moosejaw has dealt with that aspect of the case to a certain extent. In answering these two questions which I have propounded, we obtain very considerable assistance from my hon. friend who is now Solicitor General for the present Government. My hon. friend delivered a speech in this House in January, 1911. My hon, friend from Moosejaw has referred to that, and if I refer to it still farther, it is because I believe that the hon. gentleman on that occasion put up a very strong case. He adduced certain arguments and proved certain things in such a convincing way that it is unnecessary for me or any other supporter of this proposition to discuss them further. He proved that agricultural implements can be manufactured as cheaply, and as well, in Canada as in the United States. That was equivalent to showing, I think, that agricultural implements can be manufactured as cheaply in Canada as anywhere else in the world. I think every one will admit that the United States is the only serious competitor we have in the manufacture of agricultural implements such as are used in this country. I noticed that at that time there was considerable discussion of the question of reducing the duty on agricultural implements, but I do not notice that the claim of the hon. gentleman that agricultural implements could be made as cheaply in Canada as anywhere else in the world was disputed. The hon. gentleman did not ask the House to rely solely on his statements, he produced sworn evidence to prove what he said. I just wish to quote a statement made by a distinguished senator of the United States and referred to by my hon. friend the Solicitor General on that occasion. It is to be found in column 1925 of ' Hansard ' of 1911.
I would call the attention of the senators from Michigan that representatives of the International Harvester Company, who were present before the Committee of Ways and Means, said that with respect to their manufacture in Canada it cost them just as much to manufacture here; that the price of labour was the same.
I do not think anybody will dispute that, and if it is admitted that we can manufacture as cheaply in Canada as anywhere else in the world, we surely can have no just grounds for fear of outside competition. No one here will seriously claim that the agricultural implement industry is still in its infancy. It has become sufficiently strong to meet the competition of the world. The Solicitor General in the speech to which I have referred said in substance that the

object of a protective tariff was to give the manufacturing industries of Canada a reasonable hold on the home market. You will find it in column 1918 of the ' Hansard ' of that date. It was to give the manufacturing industries of Canada a reasonable hold on the home market. We have to consider the question whether or not they have a reasonable hold on the home market. If the manufacturers have not that reasonable hold on the home market it is their own fault. It has been shown by the Solicitor General in the speech to which I referred, and by my hon. friend from Moosejaw, that for a long time they have been exporting agricultural implements, that they have been exporting considerably more than we have been importing and that these exports are rapidly increasing. I am not sure if my hon. friend from Moosejaw gave the actual quotations such as were given by the hon. member for Portage la Prairie in the speech referred to. Let me quote you his record of the exports and imports of agricultural implements during the years ended March 31, 1907, and March 31, 1910. The figures adduced by my hon. friend the Solicitor General were as follows:

You will see that during these three years the exports of agricultural implements increased by something over $1,800,000, or an increase of about $600,000 per annum. My hon. friend from Moosejaw has quoted figures showing the exports of agricultural implements during the year ended March 31, 1913. He has shown that they amounted to $6,152,559. In the three years from 1907 to 1910 the increase was about $1,800,000 and we find that the increase for the three years ended March 31, 1913, was just about the same, or a little more. There has not only been an increase in past years but that increase is still continuing and the agricultural implements industry has not only a firm grasp on the home market but has also a firm grasp on the foreign market because it is able to compete with its American competitors not only in the home market but also in the foreign market. We have also had figures adduced in this House to prove that the agricultural implements manufacturers are not only able to compete in the home market and in the foreign market but right in the American home market itself.
That being so, I think it cannot be

seriously claimed that the object to which my hon. friend referred has not been attained. I think it cannot be claimed that we have not succeeded in accomplishing that object. It seems to me that the result shows that, in the first place, the agricultural implement industry of Canada has passed its infancy, that it has no need to fear outside competition and that it has a reasonable hold not only on the home market but on foreign markets. Now if that is so, all reasons and excuses for a protective policy, in so far as the agricultural implement industry is concerned, have been removed, and the object which that protective policy had in view with reference to this industry has been accomplished. If the reasons have been removed, if the objects have been accomplished, why should we have a protective policy in regard to this industry? Can any one tell? I think it goes without saying that we should not have a protective policy when, to use the argument, whether or not I use the words, of my hon. friend from Moosejaw, it' would be an iniquity to continue that policy provided the reasons were removed and the objects were accomplished. If this industry has passed its infancy* if it is able to meet, in open competition, its competitors, if the object stated by the hon. member has been accomplished, if it has a reasonable hold on the home market and also upon the foreign markets, what reason can be given why the protective policy in regard to this particular industry should be retained?
There is only one possible reason to my mind that can be given and that is in order that 'the argieultural implement manufacturers can- charge the consumers of Canada more than they charge the consumers of other countries, which has been amply proved to be the case. I have not seen a serious 'attempt to meet the arguments that have been adduced from time to time or to show that the agricultural implement manufacturers are not charging a higher price to the Canadian consumer than * to the outsider. I do not think that statement will be seriously disputed by any one. What does that mean? We are told that we should keep Canada for the Canadians. Is that Canada for the Canadians? Is charging our own consumers a higher price for what they buy than we charge outsiders to be regarded as a policy of Canada for the Canadians? Is that a patriotic policy? It is not a patriotic policy and such a policy can only be pursued by the assistance of this Parliament and that assistance must

these manufacturers been ruined by the Fielding tariff? They would not claim so now. As a matter of fact, have they not been greatly benefited by it; not directly, it is true, but indirectly? Has the country not been more prosperous, very much more prosperous, ever since the Fielding tariff was introduced, than before, and the tariff at that time had a great deal to do with making it more prosperous. The result has been that instead of the manufacturers having been injured and ruined, Canadian manufacturing has never been so successful in the history of Canada as it has been since that time.
And Sir, the result of doing what we would like to see done by this Government, would be very much the same. It would not bring ruin to the manufacturing industries of Canada, and now I do not refer alone to the abolition of the duty on agricultural implements. I am firmly convinced that if the present Government will take the necessary steps to relieve the financial situation of this country, especially among the consumers the most important class of which is the farming community; if this Government would take the necessary steps to assist-I do not like to use the term ' assist ' either-but to remove the barriers from the way of the agricultural industry of Canada, the results would be more beneficial to the manufacturers of Canada, than even the Fielding tariff was. I say that great as has been the increased prosperity of the manufacturers of Canada since the introduction of the Fielding tariff, we will see a still greater increase in their prosperity, provided the Government will do as I suggest.
We have heard a great many complaints made about the action of the late Government, and I am not here to defend the late Government. I have never defended on the platform or elsewhere the action of the late Government with regard to the tariff; I have always admitted that to my mind the decreases in the duties were not sufficient; I have never admitted at any time that the late Government had come up to my expectations in that particular. But of course, that is a question of opinion, and that was my opinion and it is my opinion still. But we have a right to deal fairly with every government, and I am willing to deal fairly with the present Government. When any one undertakes to tell us that the same tariff is in existence to-day as when the late Government was in power, I am going to ask him to take the blue book issued by the present Government, and to find out the

average rate of duty on the importations into the country before the Fieldmg tariff, and to compare them with the average rate of duty during the last year of the Liberal Administration, and I think he will find, had the same duties been collected during the year ending 31st of March, 1911, that the Government would have collected on the same importations, on the tariff that existed before the Fielding tariff; that there would be a difference of eight millions more taken out of the pockets of the people by the previous tariff.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: When the hon. gentleman made that comparison, did he take into consideration the amount of gold imports during the last two or three years?

I did not think that
gold imports were dutiable.

I would suggest to my
hon. friend that in that he may find a solution of the difficulty that is troubling him.

It is not troubling me in the least, but it is apparently troubling the Minister of Finance, and I am sorry he is in trouble. I have taken the tables published by the present Government from year to year, and I have taken the average duty on importations, and while I agree with my hon. friend that it is not an absolutely correct way to get at it, yet it is an approximately correct way. I have not made a computation for the whole time the Government was in power, but I have been told by those who have, that if a computation were made for that whole period there would have been somewhere in the neigh-bourhod of one hundred million dollars more collected on the importations into Canada by the late Government during their term of office had they collected duty at the same rate that their predecessors did. There might be a serious discrepancy for one year, I admit, but there would not be if the whole term of the Administration were taken. While a great many of us, and I among them, are not willing to admit that the late Government did all they should have done in the matter of reducing duties, I t'hink we should be fair to them and admit that they did a great deal. We would like to see the present Government go on with the same good work, and go on with it a little more rapidly.
They ^ill not do that.
