I regret that the Solicitor General is not in his place, but if he were present I do not think he would find fault with me for being sufficiently skeptical about his figures as to go into the calculation with a view to verifying them. He has made one serious error. Evidently, however, he was convinced that he was right, because in this same column he is asked a question and answers it, as follows:
Mr. Foster: What was the average valuation for 1907?
Mr. Meighen : $144.44.
Just how the hon. gentleman divides $315,744 by 2,878 and gets that quotient, I cannot understand. I have gone into it very carefully, and I find that the average valuation of a binder for 1907, instead of being $144.44, is $109.71. I do not accuse my hon. friend of deliberately misleading, but this has had the effect of misleading the public throughout the country, and that misleading has been very unfair to the late Government. I have followed this thing a little further and have made a little calculation from the Government blue books to arrive at the average duty paid on a binder in 1911. I find that the average duty on binders in 1911 was $18.25. Some one will say that that is not a material reduction; but we must consider the circumstances
before we can know whether it is a material reduction or not. In the last campaign I addressed a farmers' meeting at Fort Qu'Appelle. A farmer in the audience, clearly opposed to us, told me that the Government then in power were charging higher duties on binders than their predecessors, and to prove it he said that they valued binders at $100 where their predecessors valued them at only $80. I answered:	'I do not think that is quite
correct, but it suits my present argument.' Admit what this gentleman says as correct; the majority of us in this hall are farmers and we know something about the actual value of binders in 1896 when the Conservative Government was put out of power, and the value of binders now. Will the gentleman who interrupts me, or anybody else in this hall, undertake to tell me that the binder we buy to-day is not worth more than 25 per cent more than the binder we purchased in 1896? My interrupter sat down and he and every other opponent remained silent. Not a man would dare to say to an audience of farmers that the binder of 1911 was not worth more than 25 per cent more than that of 1896. Allow for this additional value, and we can arrive more fairly at an estimate of the reduction actually made in the duty. I take it for the year 1897, which is the one the Solicitor General took in his address. He states that for the year ending 30th June, 1897,-and I have no doubt he is correct-the average duty per binder was $20.35. Add 25 per cent to this and we get the relative duty on a binder in 1911. Therefore, had the duty not been changed,	we	would have had
to pay on such a binder as we purchase now, a duty of $25.45. Take from that the average sum we paid in the year ending March 31, 1911, which was $18.25, and you find a difference of $7.20. This is the real reduction in duty on binders made by the late Government as compared with the duty charged by their predecessors. I do not admit for a moment that that is sufficient, but I think that before the present Government find fault with the late Government they must at least do as mu-di. I think under the present circumstances, they are bound to do more. I believe, as I have stated, that the only fair way to deal with the question now, whatever may have been the case a few years ago, is to entirely abolish the duty. The object to which the Solicitor General referred has clearly been accomplished. He tells us that the object of the protective tariff is to give the manufacturing

industries of Canada a reasonable hold on the home market. They certainly have that now, and the object of protection being accomplished the need for further protection is removed. Then, why retain it? I think the Solicitor General proved a little too much for his own case; either his argument was too strong or his conclusion was not strong enough. He should have said: Abolish the duty entirely. However, I am not complaining seriously about him; I am glad he went as far as he did; it is good to have him on record. I have great confidence in the hon. gentleman.
In conclusion, it seems to me there is an obligation on the present Government to remove these duties entirely. The mere fact that the late Government did not remove the duties is not a good reason; two wrongs do not make a right, and if the late Government did wrong, that is all the more reason why the present Government should do right. But we have more reasons than that. The Solicitor General gave us encouragement to think that something would be done in this agricultural implement question. I would not speak disrespectfully in this House of Mr. Lake, my late opponent, for whom I [DOT]have the greatest respect, but when the late Government was in office I can very well remember attending a political meeting which was addressed by him. I [DOT]remember seeing a great sheet of cotton *pinned upon the wall, two or three feet [DOT]wide and twenty or thirty feet long, bearing in large letters the words: 'Vote for Labe and free agricultural implements.' 1 Believe that Mr. Lake was an honourable man; I believe that he was faithful to his party, and I refuse to believe for one moment that he would have had such a placard placed in the hall without the approval of the leaders of the Conservative party. I think we have every reason for asking the Government to carry out that pledge.
The present Government, in their wisdom 

or want of wisdom-saw fit to unite with the great manufacturers and financial interests of Canada to prevent the farmers of this country from obtaining an open market for their produce. By doing so, whatever else iwas gained by it, a terrible blow was struck at the farmers of Canada. Admitting for the moment that there was some good reason for doing this, it seems to me that the very least the Government can do is to take whatever steps they can to help the farmers in some otheT way. I

will not use the word 'compensate/ because while I submit that we have a right to expect the Government to take the necessary action, and while such action might, to a certain extent, be a compensation for the injury which was inflicted upon the farmers in connection with the rejection of reciprocity, I do not want to be quoted as [DOT]saying that the farmers of the West are prepared to accept compensation or anything else as a substitution for an open market. The present Government or any Government do all they can to improve the markets of other lines of industry; when the farmers are concerned they shut the door of the market in their faces. We have a right to free access to the markets of the world, and we will have it. This matter will not be settled until it is settled right, and it will never be settled right until we have the very .same opportunity to market our goods that other people have.

I desire, before the motion is put, to offer a few remarks upon what I consider to be one of the most important questions with which this House has had to deal during the present session. We on this side of the House, and, I fancy, some members on the other side of the House, are not quite satisfied with the wave of the hand by which the right hon. the Prime Minister sought to relegate this important matter to the ash heap, or, at all events, to some place outside the precincts of this chamber. The question is too big and too far-reaching in its consequences to be dealt with by the Prime Minister in a ten minute speech, and by the silence of the members of a party numbering 130 or 140 in this chamber. I have no doubt that there are many hon. members, supporters of the Government, who are very keenly interested in this matter- many of them representing rural ridings; many of them representing, as I do, both rural and urban populations-and who desire to give free expression to their thought and opinion upon this grave question, but who, by the wave of the hand of the Prime Minister, have been closured whether they so desire or not.
The Prime Minister took the ground-and technically, I suppose, he had the right to do so-that this matter might well wait until the Budget Speech is delivered by the Finance Minister, when any tariff changes to be made by the Government would then be announced to (the House. Had he

stopped there, I would not have had much fault to find with him. But he did not stop there. He committed himself firmly to one proposition, and that was that free implements would not be granted. He had not heard the case very fully argued; he said the Government would consider the question, but he stated, as deliberately as a man could state it in the House, that on account of the trusts and combines of the United States it would not he possible to give free agricultural implements to the people of Canada. There is only one thing left for him to do, and that is to reduce the tariff on agricultural implements to a minimum. In my view, that will not be as satisfactory as the complete abolition of the duties upon agricultural implements. But from the statement of the Prime Minister at six o'clock, his followers from the western provinces who represent agricultural constituencies, and his followers from the province of Ontario who represent the Wellingtons, the Dufferins, the Oxfords and the Water loos, can tell their constituents that the great boon of free agricultural implements has been denied to them this day by the Prime Minister of Canada, who is the mouthpiece of the Government.
Was the argument of the Prime Minister a good one? He said that the trusts and combines of the United States, those huge forces with $125,000,000 or $150,000,000 of capital, would take possession of the Canadian market df we made it free. I think my right hon. friend made that assertion without due reflection and without proper consideration. There is a free market in Great Britain, and the trusts and the combines, the tremendous organizations which manufacture agricultural implements in the United States, meet in the free market of Great Britain the manufacturers of Canada, and Canada holds her own. If these trusts cannot take possession of the British market, which is a free market, how could they take possession of the Canadian market if it were made a free market? To my mind, there is nothing dn the argument of the Prime Minister. It was not a reason for refusing to abolish the duty; it was the merest kind of an excuse.
I rose on this occasion chiefly because I think that some member from the province of Ontario should interject some remarks into this debate to show that the demand for agricultural implements is by no means limited to the western provinces of Canada. The riding which I have the honour to represent in this House is about equally made up of urban and of rural inhabitants.
I am satisfied that, irrespective of party, the people engaged in agriculture in the county of Wellington, north or south, would hold up both hands for the boon of free agricultural implements. That is so in my county and in the neighbouring counties. I wish my hon. friend from Dufferin were in his place to-night, because he knows how it is in his county. He has a county made up almost entirely of a rural population. I would put the question to him: Do your farmers not want free agricultural implements? and if there were no politics in the matter, if there was no partisanship in the matter, he would say: All the farmers in my riding want free agricultural implements. So I believe it is in the great province of Quebec and in the Maritime provinces; certainly it is in the great western provinces of Canada. From the Atlantic to the Pacific, the demand is as broad as is the country. I then ask the Government: Why not accede to a demand of that kind when your revenue is going to suffer so little and when no Canadian industry is going to be injured?
I desire in a few words to show that the removal, the entire abolition of the Canadian duties on agricultural implements, would not do an injustice to a single manufacturing establishment in Canada. The proof of that has been made plain by the hon. member for Moosejaw (Mr. Knowles), the mover of the present amendment. We in Canada export to every civilized country that uses agricultural implements we export, and we come in competition with the United States in every one of these markets. The Canadian manufacturer is able to hold his own in each of the markets to which he goes. Our only real competitor in the manufacture of agricultural implements is the United States. Other countries do manufacture them on a minor scale it is true, but our real competitor is the United States. Now, how do we compete with the United States? How do we manage to compete with the huge trusts and combines that the Prime Minister said would take possession of the Canadian market if the duty were removed? Take in the first place the relative standing of the two countries. Here we have a country vvith a population of about eight million people, while across the line there is a population claimed to be about one hundred million people. Here we have a number of very solid industries producing agricultural implements. There they have a far greater number, with a far greater capital

invested. The market of Great Britain is a free market to the world, and we meet there on equal footing, eight million Canadians against one hundred million Americans. I find that last year the United States sold there $1,023,000 worth of agricultural implements, while Canada sold one-quarter of a million worth, or about twenty-five per cent of the 9 p.m. American sales. In Australia, we meet again on an equal foot-. ing, because the tariff against Canadian implements entering Australia is precisely the same as the tariff against American implements, last year the United States sold to Australia $1,100,000 worth of implements while Canada sold to Australia $1,278,000 worth. We are a little farther away it is true, it is a little longer haul, but we sold about $160,000 worth of agricultural machinery in excess of the sales of the United States, competing there, on the other side of the world, on equal terms. Prance is another good example. The tariff against agricultural implements in Prance is the same against Canada as against the United States. To France the United States sold $2,700,000 worth. Canada sold to France $686,000, about one-quarter of the amount that the United States sold there. Take Russia as another example. United States sold to Russia $5,800,000 worth of agricultural implements. Canada sold to Russia $2,000,000, more than one-third of the sales of the United States. The most pointed example as against Canada will be the Argentine Republic. I fancy that proximity has something to do with the trade figures as between Canada and the United States when dealing with the Argentine Republic. To the Argentine the United States sold $6,000,000 worth and Canada sold $550,000 worth, a little less than ten per cent. Not only has proximity something to do with the matter tout return cargoes have a great deal to do with it. We have no steamship line from the Argentine Republic to Canada or from Canada to the Argentine, while between the Argentine Republic and the United States there are two and perhaps three lines of passenger and freight steamers, and no doubt that has a good deal to do with the larger trade of the United States. But in all the countries I have enumerated save the Argentine Republic-and I might have gone over a dozen more countries had time permitted-Canada has held her own and more than held her own. Had we done ten per cent of the United States trade we would 
have about held our own. We have done one-quarter of their trade in France, one-third of their trade in Russia and in Australia we have outstripped them by about $160,000 last year. Thus we meet on equal terms on foreign ground, Canadian and American. If we can do it there can we not do it in Canada? To my mind there is only one answer to that question. We can do it here. If the Government will abolish the duty on agricultural implements they will find that the manufacturers of these implements in Canada will thrive and prosper in the future just as they have thriven and prospered in the past. We do not need to produce the evidence, either sworn or unsworn, of any set of men to show that we in Canada are just as capable of manufacturing as they are in the United States. We have the sworn testimony, given to us in the course of this debate, that goods can be produced in Canada just as cheaply as they can be in the United States. Then why not give the manufacturers of Canada the fair opportunity of competing? They have to-day the market of the United States free of customs duty for their wares. Why, even under the tariff of last year, we sold agricultural implements to the extent of between $80,000 and $90,000, under a pretty stiff tariff to the United States. It is not always well to prophesy, but I think one may fairly say that if, in the face of a pretty fair tariff, we could sell last year from $80,000 to $90,000 worth of agricultural implements, now, with a free market of one hundred million people in front of us, this year the Canadian manufacturers will sell much more to the United States than they did last year and compete with them on their own ground.
I understood the Prime Minister to say that the United States combine in agricultural implements would invade Canada and collar our market for implements just as it had done in the case of binder twine; but it did not do so altogether in the case of binder twine. I find, on looking at the returns, that we imported from the United States last year $2,320,000 worth of binder twine. Strange as it <may seem, we exported last year to the United States $831,000 worth of binder twine, about three-quarters of a million dollars. You will find that both in our reports and in the United States trade reports. One does not need to go over the history of the tariff in regard to agricultural implements. There are a few outstanding points that we all recognize. There was a time in this country when thirty per cent and thirty-five per

cent was charged on certain agricultural implements. Gradually that very high duty was reduced and I believe at the time of the change of Government in 1896 the duty was, generally speaking, about twenty per cent. When the Liberals came into power it was reduced to seventeen and a half per cent. Three years ago there was a proposal to reduce it to fifteen per cent, that proposal forming one of the clauses in the proposed trade agreement with the United States. The history of the duty on agricultural implements has been one of gradual decline. It may be said that the manufacturers of this country have enjoyed years of protection in order that they may become well grounded in the soil of this country. I, for one, believe that of all the industries in Canada the agricultural implement industry is the one now best able to stand without the support of any customs tariff at all. I made a little list of twenty-five articles which are generally and properly considered agricultural implements. I know that some hon. members in referring to agricultural implements include only reapers, mowers, binders and a few other articles, but 1 cannot see why the list should not be much more extended. I have not included in my list such articles as axes, spades, garden tools, gas engines, wagons and the like, all of which I think might fairly be classed as agricultural implements. I find from our Canadian reports that the importation of these twenty-five articles in Canada last year amounted to $14,372,000, and that the farmers of Canada paid in duty on those articles $2,872,000 odd. Portable or threshing engines account for half that total; $7,369,000 worth of those engines were imported at a duty of $1,471,000. I believe that the portable engine on tne farm is just as much an agricultural implement as the binder or mower and for that reason I included it in my list. When I looked at the Customs tariff of Canada I was surprised to find that the rate of duty on these various articles which we usually say is I7i per cent is much more than that; it is a very small fraction below 20 per cent. Only five articles in that list bear a 17i per cent duty; ten articles bear a 20 per cent duty, four articles a 221 per cent duty and six articles a 25 per cent duty. Taking an average I found that the duty on agricultural implements is approximately 20 per cent.
Would you mind giving us the list?

I wish my hon. friend
would allow me to conclude my remarks before reading the list. There is undoubtedly in Canada to-day a demand on the part of the agricultural population for tne removal of these duties. It is said that 65 per cent of our population are engaged directly or indirectly-in agriculture. These figures probably are a little high; 60 per cent or perhaps 55 per cent would I think, be high enough, but undoubtedly the majority of Canadians are engaged directly or indirectly in agriculture, and on the part of that majority there is a demand for free implements. You hear it in the East, you hear it in the Centre and you hear it in the West. Has there been any objection to the removal of these duties? Has any deputation called on the Government to ask that the duties be maintained? I do not believe it. I believe that the manufacturers of agricultural implements, themselves, have for years seen the day coming when free implements would be admitted into Canada. They know that they can successfully compete with the United States in the markets of the world and in our market. Therefore I do not believe there has been a movement on the part of the manufacturers or any objection raised to the total removal of these duties. And yet none on the Government side of the House has had the courage to get up, in the face of a wave of the Prime Minister's hand, and advocate that the duties be removed and at this session of Parliament. If such a universal demand was made in regard to any other matter I do not believe the Government would hesitate. We have done everything for the manufacturers of agricultural implements which can reasonably be done. What goes into the ordinary agricultural implement? Iron and steel certainly. They are practically free to the manufacturer. There was 99 per cent of a drawback on all the iron and steel used up to 1907. That was only on exported implements, 'but since 1907 the drawback is upon all implements which may be made in Canada for use here or for export.

My hon. friend does
not mean that surely? That does not apply to all exports.

It applies to the main implements such as harvesters, mowers, binders and the like. It does not apply to the twenty-five articles included in my list, but to the more important and the

more numerous of those manufactures it does apply. The manufacturers practically get free iron and steel because they get a 99 per cent drawback on what they use. Then, they use wrood. Every particle of wood that goes into the manufacture of agricultural implements is free under the Canadian tariff. What else is there? There is a little paint and a little varnish. They pay duty on that. The duties run from 15 to 25 per cent and in some cases a dollar a gallon where the paint is ground in spirits. So it is, with regard to varnish. There are a few screw nails and a few bolts and they may pay a little duty on them, but that is the only duty on a machine of a value of from $150 to $175. We have done everything that reasonably could be done, we have maintained a reasonable tariff for years to give the manufacturer control of the home market. We have given him practical freedom from taxation. Now we believe that he can hold his own throughout the world and the yearly trade figures demonstrate to a conclusion that he can. Under circumstances such as these should the Finance Minister hesitate in removing these duties? The Prime Minister, by his announcement, practically said that he would not remove them. The time per- * haps has not yet come; there may be a week or two to consider this matter. I hope that in the light of these facts the Government will take this matter into their consideration. They could do no more popular act for themselves with the agricultural classes in- Canada than to make agricultural implements duty free. My hon. friend who launched this motion said that he did not do it for a partisan purpose, and that he did not ask for any credit or seek any kudos out of the matter, but that the Government might have it all. His plea was entirely on behalf of the agricultural community which he happens to represent in this House. What are the Government going to do with these facts in their possession and having at their disposal far more knowledge than we have? What is the Minister of Finance going to do with pigeon holes full of information in regard to this matter, with requests and petitions pouring in upon him month after month and week after week, not asking for a reduction from 17 to 15 or 10 per cent, hut asking for free implements? The people will not be put off with any temporizing measure. This is not the hour for reductions of the tariff; this is the time, this is the occasion, and this is the particular instance in which a tariff can be properly wiped away with the fMr. Guthrie.]
consent of the vast body of the population of Canada irrespective of politics or occupation.

Mr. Speaker; in giving my support to the amendment moved by my hon. friend from Moose-jaw (Mr. Knowles), I cannot help commenting on the remarkable way in which this amendment has been received by the members on the Government side of the House and by the members of the Government itself. As I understood it, when closure was introduced into the rules of this Parliament last year it was for the purpose of checking discussion on the part of members of the Opposition, but so far the only application of the rule that I have observed has been to the members on the Government side of the House and not to~ the members on the Opposition side. I am sure that the members of the House who were members of preceding parliaments will not have to tax their memories to any extent to recall the zeal, the enthusiasm with which hon. gentlemen on the Government side, especially those representing western constituencies, advocated a measure similar to that proposed by my hon. friend from Moosejaw, not as radical a measure, perhaps, as the total abolition of the duties on agricultural implements, but certainly a substantial reduction. I think the words ' substantial reduction ' are taken from the resolution proposed by the present hon. Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen) on the 18th January, 1911. Since this motion has been under consideration to-day, the absolute silence on the part of hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House would lead one to quote the words of the old song 'Where are the boys of the old brigade'? The boys of the old brigade are silent tonight, the hoys of the old brigade are in retreat when the question of the abolition of duties upon agricultural implements is under discussion, and when the interests of the farmers, *whom they are supposed to represent in this House and whose interest, as we know, are the dominant interests in Canada, are in issue.

Bearing in mind that
all other classes in Canada are willing to pay their share of the revenue, will my hon. friend be good enougn to tell us why the farmers of the West want absolutely free agricultural implements and decline to pay their share of the revenue?

My hon. friend is
very fruitful in questions and inter-

ruptions. I can answer my hon. friend in one word-that the premises with which he commenced his statement are, in my judgment, not correct, when he assumes that a great many people in Canada do not wish to pay their fair share of the revenue and taxation of the country. Giving a straight answer to my hon. friend's question, even if the farmer is given absolutely free agricultural implements, even if the tools of his trade, if I may use that expression, are made free, the farmer, just the same as any other consumer in the country, must still pay his fair share of taxes on everything else that he purchases for his own and his family's use. I am giving my support to this amendment for the reason, the soundness of which I think will be admitted by every member of this House, that the one basic industry of this country is agriculture. The farmers of the West and of the East are not asking for the kind of assistance that we heard proposed by an hon. member of this House yesterday, who suggested that this Government should give bounties to aid an industry that he said was in a languishing condition, namely, the iron and steel industry.
We hear hon. gentlemen opposite get up with solemn face and tell this House and tell this country that it is the duty of the Government to give bounties to the iron and steel industry. What about giving a bounty to the basic industry of all industries, namely, the digging up of the wealth of the soil th t nature has placed there, by the hands and1 by the labour of the farmers of this country. The farmers are not asking for that; all they are asking for is a square deal, and the fact of the matter is they are not getting a square deal. They are not getting a square deal from this Government, and this Government knows it. Honourable gentlemen in this House, who represent rural constituencies, know that this Government is not giving the farmers of Canada a square deal. The Solicitor General was very zealous in his advocacy of a substantial reduction of the duty on agricultural implements, when he did not have the responsibility of office on his shoulders. He is in a different position to-day; he is not a free lance any more than are the hon. gentlemen from Souris (Mr. Schaffner) and Lisgar (Mr. Sharpe).

Will the hon. gentleman
allow a question?
Perhaps the hon. gentleman will make a speech when I am through.
The hon. gentleman has said that the members of this House representing rural constituencies knew that this Government was not giving the farmers fair play.
Hear, hear.
I was one of a deputation-
You are making a speech now.
I was one of the deputation representing the farmers, who went to the Government asking them to raise the duty on farm produce coming from the United States into Canada.
What's the question?

I am delighted to have even this expression of opinion from an lion, gentleman on the other side of the House. It is evidence that in one case at least there is an hon. gentleman opposite who is able to attempt to throw off, for the time 'being, the wet blanket that the words of the Prime Minister apparently placed on the speeches and on the utterances of hon. gentlemen on that side of the House. Honourable gentlemen know, and they know it very well, that the Government is not giving the farmers of Canada a square deal; they are not giving the farmers a square deal in their demands for wider markets. There is no question of doubt but that there are gentlemen sitting on the Government side who have their position in the House to-day, and who were saved from defeat at the last election-and I see some of them before me'-who, because of their opposition to reciprocity were persona non grata with many of their constituents, were nevertheless able to persuade their constituents to vote for them by promising that, although the Conservative party was opposed to the reciprocity agreement, if the Conservative party came into power they would make' a substantial reduction in the duty on agricultural implements, if they did not abolish that duty altogether. I appeal to hon. gentlemen opposite if that is not a correct statement of the position they took during the last election. The member for Portage la Prairie-
Will the hon. member quote me when I ever said that?
I have not the newspapers at my hand-
I should think you have not.

I have not the newspapers at my hand giving the reports of the hon. gentleman's speeches, but surely I do not require that evidence when my hon. friend took such pains in this House to place himself on record, -in his own interests, supposedly in the interests of his constituents, to make the motion he did in this House in January, * 1911, in favour of a reduction of the duty on agricultural implements. Does the Solicitor-General want this House to believe that when he went on the hustings in the election following, he did not take advantage of that motion and his position on the question?
The hon. gentleman will look at that speech in vain for anything approaching what he says I stated. If the hon. gentleman be truthful I will not interrupt him.
Order.

I can tell my hon. friends here that when it comes to a question of veracity, I will stand my ground with the Solicitor-General. What I did say with regard to the Solicitor-General, and his friends of his own persuasion, was, that they held out the hope to the farmers that if the Conservative party came into office at the last election there would be a substantial reduction, if not a total abolition, of the duty on agricultural implements. I maintain that there were Conservative candidates in the West; my hon. friend from Qu-'Appelle (Mr. Thomson) inis pointed to one candidate at least, who took the position that he would support the total abolition of the duty on agricultural implements. But whether the promise was for a substantial reduction or the total abolition of the duty on agricultural implements, these gentlemen opposite, without any doubt, hold their seats in this House owing to that promise. And to-day we find them in the position that they have not a word to say on the question, and the reason is, the Prime Minister told us, because we were bringing in this amendment as a motion of want of confidence in the Government. In the name of common sense, when can a member of this House place himself on record, so far as this question is concerned? If we were to introduce this very same amendment when the Budget is brought down, and when the tariff has been settled for the coming year, we would still be guilty of introducing a motion of want of confidence in the Govern-

ment. Let me point out that when the hon. member for Rainy River (Mr. Carrick) yesterday discussed the proposition of putting a bounty on steel and iron, we did not have the same sort of answer from the Government benches that we have had from the Prime Minister to-day. The Minister of Finance was then not afraid to anticipate the Budget Speech by encouraging the member for Rainy River, in the hope that something might be done by the Government in the way of putting bounties on iron and steel. But when it comes to this demand from the farmers of Canada, that there shall be abolition of the duty on agricultural implements, the Prime Minister says to the introducer of the amendment: Sir, you are out of order, the proper place to discuss this matter is when the Budget is brought down. I preface my support of this amendment on the fact that every member of this House must recognize that farming conditions in this country at the present time are not as they ought to be. I am not going to speak so much for the farmers in Eastern Canada, with whom I am not so much in touch, as I am with the farmers of western Canada, but I say, on behalf of the farmers in western Canada, that in my judgment the motion made by the hon. member for Moosejaw (Mr. Knowles) is an opportune motion, and that the Government at this time should very justly and very fairly give us some encouragement as to what we may expect in the way of relief. My hon. friend from Moosejaw is not anxious, I am sure, to press the amendment if the Government is prepared to say, either through its Prime Minister or its Finance Minister: We have this matter under consideration, and we propose to give the farmers substantial relief. We have had no such indication, not the slightest word of encouragement, not one syllable of cheer or hope in the reply of the Prime Minister to the hon. member who moved this amendment. I say, if the Government want to put aside this motion of want of confidence, they can do it by a word, and that word is that they propose to give to the farmers what they know the farmers want and that the condition of the farmers requires-relief from the great burdens of taxation under which the farmers at least of the West are labouring.
That the conditions of the farming industry in the West are far from what they ought to be can be demonstrated in many different ways. I do not ask the

House to take my unsupported word as to that condition, but wish to give evidence that I consider as authoritative as any that can be adduced in support of the arguments I propose to make. As you are aware, Sir, something over a year ago the Government of the province of Saskatchewan appointed a commission to investigate all the conditions surrounding the industry of agriculture in that great province. It is but a couple of months since that commission compiled and presented their report. And what condition of affairs is revealed so far as the farming industry in the Prairie provinces is concerned? Why, Sir, we find an alarming condition; we find that in the year 1913, in the province of Saskatchewan while the average price received by the farmer for his wheat was 66ie per bushel, the cost of producing that wheat and getting it to market was 62c a bushel, leaving the farmer the splendid profit of 4Jc a bushel for the magnificent crop of wheat that was raised in our province last year. And the Commission give a much more favourable statement of the case than is contained in the annual report of the Bank of Commerce, an institution which, as hon. gentlemen know, has a great many branches throughout western Canada. The Bank of Commerce gives the average price received by the farmers of western Canada as 62 cents a bushel. That statement was .given in his annual report by the superintendent of western branches. Comparing the figures of 1909 and 1913, we find that while the prices for farmers' products has been rapidly decreasing, the cost of production has been rapidly increasing, so that to-day the profits of the farmer have almost if not quite reached the vanishing point. In 1909, the average price realized by the farmers of Saskatchewan for their wheat was 814 cents a bushel, against 66J cents a bushel as given by the report of the Saskatchewan Commission for 1913. On the other hand, according to that report, the cost of production has increased 12.01 cents per bushel. That, of course, is due to higher freight charges, higher terminal charges, increased cost of handling, increased cost of labour and other factors that enter into the situation. So, with decreasing prices and increasing coist of production, the farmer, even with the best crop he has had in his history, finds himself unable to do more than meet the obligations of the year without taking up a dollar of the obligations of the less successful years that have gone by.
I am free to admit that in one respect the farmers of the West have had some relief this year; but that relief has not been due to any action by this Government, but rather to the act of the Government of the United States. Live animals and certain other products of our farms have been put on the free list under the new United States tariff. And would you believe it, Mr. Speaker, such authorities as the president of the Bank of Montreal, the general manager of the Canadian Bank of Commerce, and the president of the Royal Bank of Canada, some of whom, as we remember, associated with the Minister of Finance, formed part of the ' noble eighteen ' in Toronto who took such a decided stand against the trade agreement proposed by the late Administration, and bewailed the possibility of Canadian natural products crossing the border and finding a market in the United States, to-day in their annual reports to their shareholders are actually congratulating themselves and the people of Canada on the great benefits accruing from the abolition of duties by the United States. The Minister of Finance knows what I say is true, ftfr I can give the pages in the annual reports where these admissions are made. I say I admit that it is through the act of a Government outside of this country that the farmers have received this measure of encouragement during the past six months. Nevertheless, even with that assistance, grain growing, at least under present conditions, is not a profitable business in western Canada.
No man in the country is more proud of his occupation or of his position in the community than the grain grower of western Canada. Hon. gentlemen who represent western constituencies know that full well. Yet we find that the western farmer is to-day confronted with the fact that the heads of banks doing business in eastern as well as in western Canada charge him with being more dilatory in paying his bills than the farmers of other parts of Canada. What is the reason for this ? Simply because the western farmers are so far from their ultimate market, and have to pay such excessive charges for the implements they use in developing the wealth of the soil. Unless year after year they harvest and market their crops under favourable conditions, they are bound inevitably to face the situation that is facing them today, a position almost of bankruptcy. What is my authority for these statements? I find it in the annual reports of the various banks doing business in western



Canada. The Union Bank of Canada and the Canadian Bank of Commerce have a very large number of branches in western Canada. In the annual report of the Union Bank of Canada I find this statement in reference to business in western Canada last year:
Collections are reported by manufacturers and wholesalers to be very good from the eastern province but not so satisfactory from the western provinces.
I find in the report of the Canadian Bank of Commerce this statement:
The implement companies admit that in the period of high grain prices they dispensed credit to the farmers too liberally, with the result that they have been carrying an unduly large amount of past-due farmers' paper.
That refers, of course, to the farmers of the West, because a large part of the trade done by the implement manufacturers of this country is done west of the Great lakes. The report goes on:
Consequently, at the commencement of 1913 they adopted an extremely conservative selling policy. Their conservatism was supported by the indisposition of the farmers to buy more than absolutely necessary, and in the case of heavy and expensive' machinery, such as threshers and tractors, there has been a reduction in sales of at least 65 per cent while sales of all other implements were reduced by about 33 per cent.
That is, the manufacturers of agricultural implements report that in the year 1913, in which we had our banner crop, the sales of the heavier class of implements were reduced 65 per cent and the sales of ordinary farm machinery were reduced 334 per cent.
