any recognition, favourable or unfavourable, of a resolution on this question. I may be excused for saying even this, that I doubt if it is the desire of the hon. gentleman who moved the resolution to advance the cause which he brings to the attention of the House and which he professes to have so sincerely at heart, because if that were his desire he could have adopted a no less likely way of advancing it. But if, on the other hand, his desire was to solidify in this House any opposition that might be gathered to his resolution, he could not possibly have adopted a better plan. That being the case, I am bound, as is everyone in the Government, to adhere to the statement I made in the debate on the Address and to make no comment on the merits of the resolution in so far as it affects the duty of the Government as to the tariff. That will be known in due course and what object could be served by this resolution which is an amendment to Supply I am at a loss to know, unless it be to make known to the people of Canada the very sudden conversion of hon. gentlemen opposite to freedom of duty. Perhaps it is just as well the position of hon. gentlemen opposite should be known and established. They desire to have this unanimous and in order that the idea of its unanimity should be spread broadcast they have chosen to so arrange their addresses that not only the provinces of the West but the provinces of Quebec and the province of Ontario and the province of Prince Edward Island, away in the far east have been represented in order that they might, if they possibly could, impress the whole of Canada. Two and a half years ago they were resolved that a tariff on implements ranging from 15 to 25 per cent was the lowest possible even for a revenue tariff, and also the lowest possible to keep our industries alive. Such was their firm resolve then, and such they declared it would remain in the future. But in the short space of two years they have come all the way around the circle and are now for free agricultural implements. There are two significant exceptions. I observed the rather concerned, though not altogether happy demeanour of the hon. member for South Oxford and I observed carefully that the right hon. leader of the Opposition himself has taken care to make no pronouncement whatever and has also taken care, although I hope it 
is only temporary, to absent himself from the Chamber.
The course pursued by the hon. gentlemen opposite has varied with the geography of the member who happens to be speaking. Hon. gentlemen from the West affirm their adherence to the resolution because they believe it i3 consistent with the theory of free trade, to which they profess to be permanently wedded. Hon. gentlemen from Ontario adhere to the resolution, not because it is consistent with free trade, because their representative who spoke is no free trader at all but a protectionist, and he justified his position because the manufacturers of agricultural implements are now, on the theory of protection itself, able to compete with the world and do not need the duties at all for their protection. The same position is taken by the hon. member for Beauce. He pronounced himself a protectionist this evening, with no qualification at all; and he says protection is especially necessary for infant industries. But without that condition he stated he was a protectionist in any event, although of course the necessity was greater in the case of infant industries. He was followed by the hon. member for Red Deer, who emphasized with the skill which only he possesses, the views that he pronounced; and warned the hon. member for Beauce 12 m. that inasmuch as lie was a protectionist, he was walking among pitfalls and sooner or later he would find himself upside down. I was warned in the course of the debate' on the Address that it was my duty, before I accepted the position with which I have now been honoured, perhaps over-honoured, to have secured from the Government a concession on this matter of agricultural implements, because it was one great essential that all members of the Government should see eye to eye. I think I appreciate fairly accurately the doctrine of Cabinet unanimity. I believe that on all matters of principle, whether such as relate to the tariff or to any other subject, it is essential that we should be unanimous and it is also of importance that the party behind us should be unanimous, that we should Irave some definite and well understood principle that should govern us in tariff matters. But that is a virtue and attribute that has long characterized the Conservative party. We have been able to boast of that throughout our history. But where do hon. gentlemen opposite stand ? In a position just as incongruous as that in

which they stand to-night. There must be questions and differences of opinion. Inevitably, on either side, there will be differences of opinion as to how far the principle that either side advocates will carry a party in relation to a specific duty, as, for example, how far it is necessary, with due regard to protective principles, to protect the agricultural implement industry. That, of course, is a matter of opinion, but as to the pole star that should guide our party in the matter of this duty, as of all others, there is no difference of opinion on this side of the House, none -has ever been expressed, and none exists. When, in January, 1910, I advocated the resolution so often referred to in this debate, urging upon the then Administration the necessity of reducing *substantially the duty on implements, I endeavoured, to the best of my capacity, to show that such a course was advisable. But 1 took no false ground then; I stated then that unless it could be shown that that reduction in the duties on agricultural implements was consistent with the protective principle, that it was doing fairly by all the industries of the country engaged in the manufacture of implements, I would not be a supporter of a reduction. I set about to show that that condition existed. I got little assistance from hon. gentlemen opposite. I spoke. I was followed by the hon. member -who moved this resolution to-day, and who, in the course of an hour's speech, refused to tell the House whether he favoured or opposed the resolution. He is the gentleman who is so radical to-night, and he almost shed tears in his sympathy for the western farmer as he pictured tne hard lot he suffers on the western plains. The -best that gentleman could say in favour of this 'two years ago, when he might have done something, was that he had no very great quarrel- to raise with it. Two years before that, the same hon. gentleman stated on the floor of this House, and having relation to a resolution moved by the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Schaff-ner) that the duty on binders and mowers, the chief implements, should be reduced to ten per cent. He championed the position of his party against that resolution.

I am sure my hon.
friend does not wish to misrepresent me; there was no such motion made in the House; it was in Committee.
Mr. MEIGHEN. In Committee of the Whole. lOli
A wonderful difference.
A great difference.

We must all admire the pliability of conscience of the hon. member. It is very important to the constituents of Moosejaw that he take a proper position on the floor of the House, but if the House i->
in Committee of the Whole, it matters very little. I was rather struck by one of the arguments adduced by the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie). He urged that inasmuch as the implement manufacturers were seizing a considerable share of the foreign trade and succeeding there, that was an argument that they required no protective duty in Canada. Is the memory of the hon. member for Moosejaw long enough to admit that in the course of his speech in the House against the resolution of the hon. member for Souris, he took the ground that the fact of the implement manufacturers succeeding in foreign trade was a reason why we should not reduce the tariff at all? The hon. gentleman shakes his head and is not aware of it. I will read it to him, (page 5598, ' Hansard,' 1907):
The manufacturers * of agricultural Implements must certainly undersell the other manufacturers of the world or they must compete with them at least. They can do so either by cutting prices or by selling in the open market at the same price as they are selling in Canada. If they do so by selling at cut prices, it is no argument in the mouth of the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) that the agricultural implement makers can stand on their own footing. If they sell in foreign markets at the same price as in Canada then they can compete with their competitors and the removal of this duty' would make no difference at all. .	. If the Canadian manufacturers compete in the world's markets their price must be just as low, and there would be no object whatever in reducing the duties further.
My hon. friend is just giving part of that speech. I was making a hypothetical statement.
There is nothing hypothetical about this.
Look again,

It is not hypothetical at all, but it may bear analogy to another word of a similar sound.
If the Canadian manufacturers compete in the world's markets their price must be just as low, and there would be no object whatever in reducing the duties further.
Where is the hypothesis?
The word ' if '.
The hon. member now says that if the manufacturers are able to compete in the world's markets, we should sweep the duties off altogether. I do not see how the two doctrines can sleep together.
What are you going to do about it?

The hon. member foT Carleton knows that no government worthy of the name of government could possibly make an announcement before the Finance Minister announces his Budget. Perhaps he will get it too soon for his comfort. The hon. member for South Wellington first of all entered a bitter complaint against the shortness of the speech of the right hon. the leader of the Government. He declared this subject was of such vast consequence, not only to the western farmers but to the whole Dominion, that it was nothing short of an insult to the mover of the resolution to dismiss it in a fifteen minute speech. But he got past that argument and forgot his initial position. Later on he complained that the speech of the right hon. the leader of the Government was too long altogether, and that if he had stopped as soon as he had stated that the position of the Government was one of reserve, waiting for the proper time in this as in other matters, then he would have found no fault with the right hon. gentleman at all. That is just where the right hon. the leader of the Government did stop. The Prime Minister made no pronouncement whatever on the merits of the resolution as affecting the tariff. He stopped just where the hon. member for South Wellington said he should have stopped. In the course of the speeches of hon. gentlemen opposite I have observed: it was complained of very bitterly by the member for Humboldt (Mr. Neely) and was followed, rather to my astonishment by the hon. member for Red Deer, who cannot often be charged with lack of information, although he can sometimes be charged with a lack of logic -that now that the American tariff was removed on implements we were not setting about to remove our tariff as well. He said: ' It is true, in 1911 we had an election in this country and the country at that time rebuked the late Government when they set about to reduce the tariff by two and a half per cent, and the Conservative party made a successful appeal to the country notwithstanding the attitude of the Government with regard to reciprocity, but at that time there was an 
American tariff on implements, which made all the difference in the world.' Expressing it more forcibly as he can do, the hon. member for Red Deer said: 'That is the crucial point, the whole thing turns on that; we have now a slaughter market across the line; in 1911 we were without this slaughter market.' Has the hon. member for Red Deer forgotten that at the very time the reciprocity treaty was being negotiated there was a clause in the American tariff providing that if we threw down our tariff we should get their slaughter market? The countervailing clause stated, that if, at any time, we put implements on the free list their implements went on the free list automatically. So that the American market was open to us in 1911, just the same as now.
Had the Americans not a duty on implements then?

Yes, but my hon. friend understands what a countervailing clause is. He understands it, at all events, when talking about free wheat. Why cannot he understand it when talking about free implements? The Minister of Finance of that day stated in the House that our representatives in the reciprocity negotiations were offered free entry for our implements into the United States if we allowed implements free into Canada. I can appeal with some confidence to the hon. member for Red Deer, now that he sees that the whole bottom is out of his case.
I must really object to my hon. friend putting words into my mouth. I did not say anything of the kind.
No one is so blind as he who will not see.
That is a different statement from what you made a minute ago.

The hon. gentleman sees, if he will do justice to his intelligence, that the late Government were in a position to get the American market just as free as it is to-day to this Government. So that the position of the two cases is exactly the same. It is not only analogous but it is exactly alike.

I am sure that my hon. friend does not want to misrepresent me. I took these two positions: one is that we have a slaughter market in the United States. I compared that position with the time when, for years, my hon. friend and his friends used the argument that we could not reduce duties on

this side because we should be made a slaughter market by the Americans. The difference between then and now must be obvious to any one who wants to approach the question with anything but the hairsplitting ability for which my hon. friend is so famous.
Then and now! The then that the hon. gentleman spoke of was two years ago, when the reciprocity campaign was on.
No
Yes; and he told us that what we got votes upon was the slaughter market in Canada being open to the United States.

I must correct my hon. friend. I said distinctly that for years and years that was the hon. gentleman's argument, and I did not mean to confine my statement to the last general election. If the hon. gentleman does not wish to be unfair he will accept my statement.

I do not wish to be unfair. Perhaps I should be satisfied now that the hon. gentleman has admitted that two years ago the opportunities of the late Government were just exactly the same as the opportunities of this Government today.
The hon. gentleman will not admit that?
The position is not the same; .the duties are gone in the United States.
The duties are gone, but they tried to get them gone two years ago; so it is just exactly what this Government is asked to do to-day.
Well, take the opportunity then.

So the hon. gentleman does admit it, and he will be prepared to castigate his leader just as severely as he will castigate the leader of the present Government if the leader of the present Government does not accede to the resolution, or to its effect, when the proper time comes. The conversion of hon. gentlemen opposite is a most striking tribute to somebody. I would not like to take it to myself, although they have done me the honour of quoting very freely from my speech of January, 1911. The conversion of hon. gentlemen opposite is one of the
most striking things in their history, and that is saying quite a lot. The hon. gentle-man says that there has been an advance in the Liberal party. I know that he believes that. He is preaching the gospel of free trade, and he is in earnest. I have no doubt that he believes it is somewhat due to his own missionary work and proselytism that this great advance has taken place. I congratulate the hon. member for Red Deer on the disciples around him who appear to be multiplying very rapidly. But while I offer him my congratulations let me also give him this little word of warning that if he should ever live-and I doubt very much his capacity to do so-until his friends around him are again in power in Canada, he will find a very material defection from the ranks of the free-traders. He will find his hopes dashed to the ground very suddenly as the hopes of all who professed to believe in his principles were dashed very suddenly in 1896. In 1911, just two years ago, or a little more, not only did hon. gentlemen opposite refuse the offer of the United States to allow our implements into their country free if we would allow theirs into this country, but they refused it, because, in the words of the Finance Minister, responsible for the tariff policy, it would be doing an injustice to the implement manufacturers of Canada. They refused it because it would not be consistent with the protective principle which they followed but refused to profess. Now they are free traders on agricultural implements. But worse than that; in reducing binders and mowers from 174 per cent to 15 per cent, in reducing many other implements from 20 to 15 per cent, and others from 25 to 20 per cent, and in leaving traction engines and threshing machines exactly where they were, not only did they say they were doing that but that was all they would do, and that they had no intention in the future of going any farther. The hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) knows what I am coming at now. I can see it in his face. He is the hon. gentleman who said this in a speech in Woodstock quoted in the Toronto Globe of the 4th March, and not one word of which he will deny to-night.
Let us hear it.

He could not see that the manufacturers would he touched very much, as few articles manufactured in Canada were affected. He was sure the Bain and Woodstock wagon companies would compete in the world's markets even with 2J per cent reduction in the tariff.

He thought the manufacturers opposed reciprocity because of what might follow, the ' thin end of the wedge but he had been assured by Sir Wilfrid Laurier and Mr. Fielding that nothing of the sort would follow. They had gone as far in the farmers' interests as they would.
The right hon. leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) is in the House, and I know that he will not repudiate the statement then made by the hon. member for North Oxford, because when it was .attributed to the hon. member for North Oxford on the floor of the House, ' Hansard,' page 5742, the hon. gentleman, who was then the leader of the Government, now the leader of the Opposition, made this statement:
The statement made by the hon. member for North-Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) was quite consistent with our policy, it was nothing new, and he had perfect authority, not only he but every member of the Liberal side, to make that statement.
Mr, Foster:	Did the Prime Minister and
the Minister of Finance authorize the member in question to make that statement?
Sir Wilfrid Laurier:	I have answered that
already. It is perfectly true. The hon. member for North Oxford and every Liberal member had such authority, he was not kept in ignorance of our policy in this matter and knew it well. He only stated what is our general policy.
If the declarations of the hon. member for Moosejaw and the hon. member for Red Deer are correct that the Liberal party in the House of Commons are unanimous, now that they are in Opposition, that we should sweep the whole duty off agricultural implements, are they quite consistent with the statement of the right hon. leader of the party two years ago? Two years ago he warned the people of this country in most pronounced terms that it should not be regarded as the thin end of the wedge if they took 24 per cent of the duty off implements. It was not the thin end of the wedge but the whole wedge because they had no intention whatever of going any further. However, my hon. friend from Red Deer is surely to be congratulated that he has persuaded his leader, the hon. member for North Oxford and other hon members of the Liberal party, that they were entirely wrong in 1911, that they did not know anything about the real virtue of free trade but that now that he has opened their eyes they can, after two years of irresponsibility, advocate absolute free trade in agricultural implements.
My hon. friend from Red Deer seems to be of the opinion that there have been emissaries down here from the implement manufacturers persuading the Government not to dare to touch the duty on imple-[Mr. MeiffhenJ
ments. In that, he seems to have different information from the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie), who took the ground that none of the implement manufacturers would dare to ask for anything except what they were granted; that nobody, either among the manufacturers or farmers was asking for anything else, and therefore he urged upon this Government the great popularity of the move they would make if they only accepted the resolution of the hon. member for Moosejaw (Mr. Knowles). I do not know whether the hon. member for South Wellington is correct, or whether the hon. member for Red Deer is correct-they are each at opposite ends of the tether-but I have not seen anybody down here interviewing the Government.
I have seen an hon. gentleman hovering around, who was a prominent Liberal in the constituency of North Waterloo, and I ' rather -suspected his purpose was to try and convert hon. gentlemen opposite to his views on tariff matters. I do not know what his effect on hon. gentlemen opposite was, but he was down here, and ;so far as I know he was the only -one who was here. But this Government takes the ground that they are here representing, not one class but all of the great interests of this country. Be they the farmers, be they the manufacturers, or be they anybody else, they are at liberty to see this Government and to present th-eir views, and fair and just treatment will be meted out to them. The country is in the position of knowing now what is the talisman, what is the guide, that will determine the course of this Government. Th-e country also knows that were hon. gentlemen opposite to be returned to power, no man could discern and no man could describe the principles that would govern them. The hon. member for Moosejaw, when he was on his feet, when challenged to say what system of tariff was put into effect toy the Liberal party, refused 'to answer the challenge. He was asked by the hon. member for North Grey (Mr. Middlebro) if he would kindly tell the House what system of tariff was put into effect by Sir Wilfrid Laurier when he came into power, and his answer was that he thought * it was the duty of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Middldbro) not to interrupt. And so, I say, the country has the advantage now of knowing what the principle is that is going to govern it, and I believe the people will say that that principle will be fairly applied in justice to all concerned.

It was the Conservative party, and not the Liberal party, that effected the greatest reduction in the duty on agricultural implements. The progenitors of hon. gentlemen opposite, if I may use the expression, when in power 1873 to 1878, established a tariff of 171 per cent, and decided that that was the lowest they could go, in justice to the revenue; but hon. gentlemen opposite now think they can go to nothing and still do full justice to the revenue. That tariff of the Mackenzie Government was raised under the national policy until at became virtually a tariff of 35 per cent, but two years before the Conservative party went out, in 1896, it was reduced to twenty per cent. Let me remind the House that in the whole course of fifteen years of power, hon. gentlemen opposite succeeded only in shaving two and a half per cent off these duties. They never shaved a cent off until they had ibeen in power for eleven years, and they did that, notwithstanding the advocacy of individual members, because individual members may hold different views as to the application of a principle. They continued the duty for eleven years, notwithstanding the pledged word of a man, most specifically made, who was a member of the Government practically throughout these eleven years, and who stood on the platforms in western Canada and pronounced himself in favour of, and promised solemnly to the people: free coal oil, free agricultural implements, free clothing, and free many other things. He particularly specified agricultural implements, and never ceased to specify them, and on the placards that covered the bill-boards thro agh-out his constituency, yes and throughout the province, he endorsed the promise to the people of that province that they should have free agricultural implements. Notwithstanding all that, hon. gentlemen opposite maintained the duty exactly as it was, for eleven years after they came into office. So that it will be received with very little concern by the people of Canada to-day, just what these gentlemen opposite promise now, two short years after they have been hurled from power.
I think the people of Canada will believe that they can look forward with more confidence and with more certainty, to w'hat will be done in tariff matters by a Government whose prinicples they know, rather than by a band of politicians, composed partly of long-distance free traders, and partly of mushroom protectionists.

I wish to say a word, not altogether in reply to what the Solicitor-General has said, because I think we have had the good fortune to listen to him at his very best, in that he has been able to talk for thirty-five minutes and not say anything, thus carrying out to its proper conclusion the closure announcement made by the Prime Minister, when he spoke before six o'oclock. We are interested, of course, in the constitutional aspect of the proceedings now before the House. There is a saying that loyalty is the last refuge of scoundrels, and it seems to me that the constitution is the last refuge of our friends on the other side. Whenever they are in particular trouble, they at once take refuge in the constitution, and when a great question is brought up for the consideration of this House-and I take it that the purpose for which this House is created is for the discussion and consideration of great questions and decision thereon- when a great question is brought before the House for its consideration, in a manner entirely in accord with the rules of the House, the Solicitor General sprains his thinker in explaining that there is some infraction of the constitution in the course that is being taken; and that in fact, these gentlemen who were elected to support the hon. gentleman are not at liberty to think or speak or pronounce their judgment on that question; that they must not say anything; that they must- not have anything to say-
And that they must not think.

Or, that they must keep
their thinks to themselves. I take issue, and I think all on this side will take issue with the Solicitor General and his leader on that point. We believe that the purpose of Parliament is that the representatives of the people of Canada met here shall consider these matters that are of most interest to the people of Canada, according to the rules of this House. And, if the matter is to be argued later on, I think my hon. friends opposite will find that it is a very poor defence, in excusing themselves for voting against the interests of the people of Canada, when the vote is taken, that they have followed the direction of the Prime Minister and of the Solicitor General.
After dealing with the poor old constitution, the Solicitor General next impugned the motives of gentlemen on this side of the House-he mentioned particularly, I think, the member for Moosejaw who moved the resolution-and he suggested that the leader

of the Opposition was out of the House because he did not wish to have a part in the consideration of the question. I think my hon. friend sized himself up when he made that suggestion. He has made some explanation to the House in regard to what other members have said on the question of. the duties on agricultural implements. He has not had so much to say in regard to what he himself said. And, after all, it does not matter so much what he said as what he did. In January, 1911, he moved a resolution in this House, and supported it with, I must say, a very able and well-reasoned speech in favour of reducing the duties on agricultural implements-I do not suppose he will deny that that was the purport of his resolution and the logical sequence of his speech. But when the opportunity came to him in 1911 to vote in favour of a reduction in the duty on agricultural implements, he voted against it. I presume that his action in 1911 will concur with his action in 1914. But if it does not, he is even then only following his own record. He has been challenged here this evening, he and his friends on the other side, on the point that his speech on agricultural implements and the adherence given to those remarks by his friends on that side secured their election' in a number of cases. It will be for us to judge as to their sincerity when the Budget is brought down. Whoever else may challenge the motives of speakers on this side of the House in regard to the duty on agricultural implements, I submit it is not for my hon. friend to do so.
He suggested that the members on this side had made a sudden conversion to the idea of lower duties or the abolition of duties on agricultural implements. Is the Government that we have in power to-day a Government that takes no account of conditions as they exist or conditions as they change? Is it to be really a Tory Government, one that stands by what is because it was and takes no Tegard of conditions as they change for better or for worse? What matters it to the country to-day what the Liberal party did in 1911? What the country wants to know is what the Conservative party is going to do in 1914. There were certain conditions existing in Canada in 1911 which conditions are absolutely reversed in 1914. Let the Liberal party be right or wrong in what it did then, the question is, what is the Government of the day doing to meet the conditions as they exist to-day which conditions are so radi-fMr. Oliver. ]
ealty different from what they were in 1911 and are of a character startling to anybody but a Government which, apparently, believes that the whole duty of a Government is to collect taxes and spend them.
The hour is la.te, but still I hope I may be pardoned if I occupy a few minutes in drawing the attention of the House to the change of conditions to which I allude, in which change consists the urgency of the case, and which, I think, I shall be able to impress upon the country if not upon the members of the Government. It has been said here already that the agricultural industry is the great industry of Canada. I may say that the agricultural industry of Canada is chiefly located to the three Prairie provinces.
Oh, no.

Well, I will say that at any rate. And I do not think my hon. friends, if they consider the matter for a moment, will contradict the position, In these Prairie provinces we have disposed of 154,000,000 acres of land, the greater part of it having been selected because of its fertility and suitability for cultivation-an area greater than that of the Empire of Germany, nearly as great as that of the Empire of Austria, equal to that of the Republic of France. Out of that stupendous area, 17,500,000 acres was in cultivation in 1911. In 1901, the area under cultivation was 2,500,000, and the increase of the area under cultivation from 2,500,000 acres in 1901 to 17,500,000 acres in 1911 is what has created the condition of advancement that did exist throughout Canada in the year 1911. The crop of 466,000,000 bushels of grain last year, worth, according to the statement of the Bank of Commerce, $180,000,000, constitutes the agricultural industry of the western provinces-I speak of the grain-growing merely-by far the largest factor in the creation of wealth in this Dominion of Canada. It is because of the rapid increase in the creation of that wealth during the ten years from 1901 to 1911 that Canada has achieved the position that she has achieved, commercially, industrially, financially, and in other ways.
How much has Canada increased industrially ?

My hon. friend will excuse me; just at the moment I have not all the figures he requires under my hand, but I am giving the figures as to the increase of agricultural production in the period that I have mentioned. I say that

that production could not exist; that wealth could not be created, without its having an enormous effect upon the general welfare, prosperity and progress of the country. We had, I say,	a production
of $184,000,000 worth in the prairie provinces last year-occupying only 12 per cent of the area of land that we have disposed of for development. There are, therefore, before the Dominion of Canada the possibilities that would necessarily and naturally flow from the continuation of cultivation until the whole 150,000,000 acres is occupied and improved. There is the possibility of making Canada as great in population or in wealth as any of the great countries of Europe, with their forty, fifty and sixty millions of people and their hundreds of millions of dollars of wealth. But in order to do that we must have continued increase in that cultivation, and in order to have continued increase in cultivation there must be profit to the producer from that cultivation. From the year 1911 to the present time, because of a lack of profit to the producer, the area of production has been decreasing. The demand for land has gone down, and this country is face to face with a condition not of expansion but of contraction. It means that this whole country stands in danger of commercial paralysis because of the failure of the crop of the prairies to give a profit to the producer.
Up to a certain point the price of wheat was rising on the world's markets; since 1910 the price of wheat has been going down on the world's markets. This Government cannot control the world's markets, but it can take measures to reduce the costs of production and transportation, thereby securing a measure of profit where otherwise no profit would exist. To reduce the cost of production it is proposed to reduce the cost of the implements with which the production is secured, and it is because there is an urgent necessity in the interests of the whole Dominion of Canada that this cost of production shall be brought down so that a profit may accrue to the producer, that the proposal to abolish the duties on agricultural implements is placed before Parliament. There is only one market for the surplus wheat of the world: in Great Britain, Germany, and some of the smaller European countries. To fill that marfcet there aTe the exporting countries, amongst which are Argentina and Australia, where the conditions are similar to those in our own prairie' west,
and where vast areas, just as vast as ours and measurably as productive, await development. If we are not prepared to produce from our western plains at a rate that will enable us to reach the European market in competition with Australia and the Argentine, not to mention the rest of the world, Australia and the Argentine will develop and Canada will stand still, just as Canada stood still under the policy of high tariff from 1884 until 1896. Our homestead entries have gone down; they were 10,000 less in the year ended March 31, 1913, than they were in the year ended March 31, 1911. Land sales have gone down from 19,000,000 acres in 1911 to 9,000,000 acres in 1913. That is a matter that will interest even my friend the Minister of Finance and those who are associated with him. The security for their money is being depreciated by present conditions. There must be a policy of taking the burdens off the farmers' backs or they cannot produce at a profit, and if they cannot produce at a profit they cannot produce at all, and this whole country of Canada loses that vitality that has flowed through it from those prairies during the	ten
years of which I	speak,	and the
consequence must be stagnation such as we had in Canada in those former years. The idea seems to have been that because the country was settling up rapidly, because production was increasing rapidly, that therefore the farmer was getting rich, and everybody was in line to take a bite out of him. It was not only the agricultural implement dealers. The farmer of the West has to buy a large part of the food that he uses. Although he raises wheat he has to buy flour. Fruit he does not raise, and therefore he has to buy it in whatever form he can get it. It may interest some of our friends to know that as a result of a break in the price of canned goods prices have come down so that tomatoes, which sold last year at fifteen and twelve and a half cents per can, are now sold for ten cents or three cans for a quarter. Peas, which sold last year for twelve and a half, fifteen and twenty cents, are to-day sold at fifteen cents for first quality, and three for twenty-five cents for second. The prices have gone down this year, but the prices were up last year as a result of the operations of the canners' combine, and have been a. load to be carried by the farmer of the West, increasing the cost of his living and decreasing the profit of his operations.
Are you finding fault with the price of canned goods this year?

I am finding fault with
the prices to which my hon. friend put them up last year and the previous year; and we do not thank him for their being lower this year; they are lower because he cannot help it.
Why?
I cannot say why, I am only saying that it is the case that he cannot help it.
Have crop conditions got anything to do with it?
I do not know.
You do not know anything about what you are talking about.
The crop conditions had nothing to do with the prices the previous year.
I think they had all to do with them.

Then we disagree. It was the fact that the hon. gentleman and his friends formed a merger of the canneries of Ontario, they had watered the stock and were intent upon earning a dividend on that watered stock and the farmers in the West had to pay the price. The reason the prices are lower this year is because the independent canners have
1 a.m.	bucked the combine.
Take the duties off and they will go down further still.

I may inform the hon.
gentleman that we are selling canned goods to the United States.
Then you would be willing to take the duty off?
He says that the combine is robbing the people of the West, and I tell him that we are shipping to the United States.

They certainly have been robbing the people of the West, and I say that if they are not doing that now it is because their power was broken by the independent canners, according to the authority I have here. But it is not only in the West that this condition exists. I have here an article by a gentleman whose word will not be questioned as being an expert in the matter. Mr. J. W. Elavelle, has been enlightening the people of Canada in regard

to matters concerning food, and I am sure everybody will agree that nobody knows more about it than Mr. Flavelle. In the course of a long article he says:
The census of 1911 as compared with that of 1901 shows that there was a decline of 96,000 in the number living upon the farms in this province.
It is not only in the western provinces that the agricultural conditions have been unfavourable; they have been correspondingly unfavourable in the eastern provinces. There are fewer people on the land in the province of Ontario to-day than there were ten years ago, according to Mr. Flavelle.
Mr. WM. SMITH: Bead the whole of it.
We have not time. It is all very interesting and I recommend my hon. friend to read it. It is published in Saturday Night of February 28.
Bead the whole of it.

I was pointing out that a condition which affects the welfare of this whole country is imminent and calling for legislative action without delay; that action is necessary in the interests, not of the western farmer but in the interests of this whole country; that the condition to-day is absolutely reversed from what it was in 1911. Up to that time we had a continual increase in cultivation, in settlement, in homestead entries, in everything that related to the progress of the country. Since that day we had a continual decrease in cultivation, in homestead entries, in values of land. Is the Government not going to recognize that condition? Are they not going to recognize the necessity of reducing the cost of production in the West, and in the East as well, by any and every means that lie to their hand. Instead of giving interesting disquisitions in regard to the shortcomings of members on this side of the House, it is in order for our hon. friends to busy their minds with the necessities of the country and to make provision for meeting those necessities. It is no doubt of great interest that Mr. So and So on the Liberal side said such and such a thing at such and such a time, but it is very much more interesting to know that the members of the Government and the members who sit behind them have a just appreciation of the facts and conditions as they are, and are prepared to take adequate measures to meet those conditions. And before leaving this, let me suggest that to read an extract from the remarks made in the House by an hon. gentleman may or may not convey a correct

impression of the ideas which he was giving to the House at the time. It depends upon how the extract is taken out.

Has that any special
reference?

It has a very special reference to the suggestions that my hon. friend was putting before the House tonight in regard to the remarks that he read from speeches made on previous occasions, and to his remarks in regard to the action or inaction of the Liberal Government in regard to reduction of duty at the time of the reciprocity agreement.
What did I leave out?

The reciprocity agreement covered a vast field of interest and endeavour, and when my hon. friend takes one particular item and says you did not do so -and so in regard to that it is true we did not, but we were doing something else in regard to other matters. We were giving a free market in the United States to the Canadian producer for everything that he raised. I am not so sure, if my hon. friend would make that arrangement for us to-day, that we would not accept a moderate reduction in the duty on agricultural implements. But the trouble is my hon. friend will not give us the market for our products, and I am afraid he will not give us a reduction on implements either. We have no apology to offer for the reciprocity agreement in any particular. It was an arrangement intended to meet conditions as they then were, in regard to markets for our western producers and in regard to the cost of living to the people of Canada. It is true that at that time those questions were not so pressing as they are to-day but they were in sight, and the Government of that day proposed to deal with them. It is not a question of prospect to-day, the problems are here, facing us, and demanding the attention of the Government; and I say that the electors of this country will not clear the Government of responsibility because of clever suggestions and quotations by my hon. friend or his leader. They have a responsibility, they have to provide for the welfare of this country, and the shortcomings or faults of their predecessors have nothing to do with the case. They have a responsibility and an opportunity and they will be judged on how .they discharge that responsibility and how they take advantage of that opportunity, and not on what they say about us.

I propose to bring some matters to the attention of the Government which have not yet been touched upon. I did not have an opportunity to speak when the question of free wheat was being discussed, but I do not propose to let this opportunity pass. As this question is of great importance I think it is up to every western member to state where he stands on this matter of protection. I was surprised to hear the Prime Minister complain that this question bad been brought in, in the manner it was, but I can remember, and you can remember, Mr. Speaker, that in the year 1910, just before what was described as ' The Invasion ' of Ottawa by the western representatives and the organized farmers, you yourself, Sir, brought in a resolution which will be found on page 1196, asking for the same thing that the western delegation came here to secure. You brought in a resolution asking that something be done towards establishing cold storages and other things. The Prime Minister complains that this resolution has been brought in before the Budget, but that resolution to which I referred was brought in on the 13th December, many months before the Budget was brought down.
What has that to do with the tariff?

If my hon. friend will wait I will tell him. The Prime Minister complains that the resolution of my hon. friend from Moosejaw has been brought in before the Budget. I -say that the hon. gentleman who is now the Speaker of the House brought in a resolution in advance of the presentation of the Budget and that it was supported by the present Prime Minister, then leader of the Opposition. He voted in favour of that resolution which was brought in many months prior to the bringing down of the Budget by the Government of the day. I am not going to argue as to the merits or demerits of the resolution which was then brought in by the hon. member for North Grey but I will say that there is nothing irregular about the resolution brought in by my hon. friend from Moose-jaw. Keeping in mind other resolutions which have been brought to the notice of the House, and which have been promised consideration by the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. White) on behalf of tne Government, I think that every hon. member representing an agricultural constituency in this House has a good reason for supporting the resolution brought in by my

hon. friend from Moosejaw. The western farmers, and I am a western farmer, have been advised by the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Foster) that he should go into mixed farming. This resolution has a good deal to do with going into mixed farming. Every man who knows anything about it must know that wheat farming and mixed farming are almost two different occupations. A wheat farmer can get along with 160 acres of land and one wagon, whereas if he is a mixed farmer, he will probably use two wagons. This necessitates an increase in his expenditure and the matter of duties is one of very great concern to him. The duty is 25 per cent on wagons and if a man is obliged to buy two wagons instead of one because of the extra amount of hauling that will be necessary in the feeding of cattle, it will cost him an extra $40 instead of $20. The Minister of Trade and Commerce tells us that we are ruining the land, that we should go into mixed farming and that we should fertilize the land by putting more cattle upon it. The man who embarks upon mixed farming would require to purchase a manure-spreader, a very expensive implement which, under the tariff, pays a duty of 20 per cent. It costs in our country about $200. There is $40 of an outlay that has to be made by the mixed farmer that the wheat farmer is not called upon to make. Therefore, if we follow the advice of the Minister of Trade and Commerce we have to purchase an extra wagon and a manure-spreader. If the advice of that hon. gentleman is good we will have to put stock upon the land which will produce fertilizer and that naturally will necessitate a machine to distribute that fertilizer.
The difference in the price of a wagon manufactured in Canada and one manufactured in the United States is about $35. Those who have had experience in the matter find that it is better to pay $105 for an American wagon than to pay $85 for a Canadian wagon. The Canadian wagon makers do not attempt to come up to the American standard at all. They put a cheap wagon on the market and the lower price attracts a good many purchasers, the workmanship is as good in one as it is in the other, but the material in the Canadian wagon is not as good as that in the American wagon notwithstanding the fact, as was pointed out by my hon. friend from South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie), that the wood used in the manufacture of this wagon 
comes in duty free. The Canadian manufacturer takes advantage of the tariff which enables him to manufacture a cheaper article and one which he can sell for $85. The two wagons are the same as far as the layman may be able to judge but while one sells for $85 the other is sold for $105. Tne American wagon at $105 is the better of the two. I have had both of these wagons on my farm. I do not wish to name any particular make of wagon but I have found that it is cheaper to buy a wagon at $105 than to buy a wagon of Canadian manufacture at $85. Therefore, if we adopt the advice of the Minister of Trade and Commerce and go into mixed farming it necessitates the purchase of another wagon which will cost us from $20 to $25 extra on account of duty. Then, as I have said, a manure-spreader costs about $200 in our country and the duty on. a manure-spreader is 20 per cent. Therefore, the farmer who takes the advice of the Government of the day will have to pay $40 or more in order that the Canadian implement manufacturers may be protected. I am told by American citizens that they can buy a manure spreader in the United States for from $50 to $60 less than we have to pay for the same implement in Canada. If we are to take the advice of hon. gentlemen opposite as a panacea for the troubles and hardships that we have to encounter in the West we will have to pay out $50 or $60 for the protection of the manufacturers of Canada in addition to what we would have to pay if the proposition of my hon. friend from Moosejaw were adopted.
A lot of money has been expended on agricultural education since this Government came into power, and in sending out their pamphlets from the Department of Agriculture, they have recommended the use of packers in western Canada, but packers cost to-day in Canada $60 more than they cost in the United States. Here are three articles required in mixed farming: wagons, manure spreaders, and packers; and why should the Canadian farmer have to pay to-day so much more for these implements than he would have to pay in the United States? During the reciprocity debate in 1911, it was a strong argument of the Conservatives that whether reciprocity came into force or not it would make no difference in the price of farm machinery, because the American combines would force the prices up. About the only election pamphlets that were sent out in Alberta, contained a statement from the Hon.

Clifford Sifton that if reciprocity came into force we would become the back yard of Chicago, and he stated that if we were to take the duty off farming implements we would get into the clutches of the American combine, and would have to pay more for them than we do at the present time. The same argument was used by these gentlemen with regard to the duty on cattle going into the United States, but when the duty on cattle was removed by the Americans, the farmers of the West got a bigger price for their cattle by at least $10 per head. I take the following statement from the Calgary Herald, a well-known Conservative organ, which ought to be accepted as an authority by gentlemen on the other side:

We were told by the Conservatives during the campaign in 1911 that if our cattle were allowed free into the United States markets it would not increase the price to the farmers, but here we find from the figures published in a newspaper friendly to the Government, that the cattle sent from Alberta to the United States brought
ten dollars a head more than the cattle sent to British Columbia and to Winnipeg.
Why didn't they all go to the United States P

I will tell you why: it is because the removal of the American duty on cattle did not come into force until near the end of the year, and if it had come into force before, the prices of Alberta cattle in Winnipeg and British Columbia would have been $91 a head instead of $81.
I believe that the statements we on this side of the House make to-night to the effect that if the duty is taken off agricultural implements they will be purchased at a lower price by the western farmer than they can be purchased to-day, will be as true as the statement we made in the campaign of 1911 that if the duty were removed on cattle going into the United States, and if reciprocity came into force, our farmers in the West would realize higher prices on their cattle. I know men in the West who have friends coming from eastern Canada and from the eastern States, who are buying their machinery in eastern Canada and using it for a certain length of time there, and then shipping it to the West, and making considerable money on the transaction. There are a lot of small implements used on the farm that people from the United States settling in the West find it more profitable to buy in the United States even though they have to pay the duty. Speaking as a western farmer, I submit to the House that if we have to compete in the world's market to find buyers for what we produce, it is up to us to start fair in the matter of production. Everybody knows that agricultural implements in the United States are cheaper by just the amount of the duty. If it were not for the duty our American friends who are settling on the prairies to-day would send to the United States for 'their agricultural machinery. It has been shown here to-night that the Canadian manufacturer is able to compete m foreign markets, and that being so, he should certainly be able to compete at home. This Parliament has no right to take the money of the farmers whose industry has been rightly described as the foundation of the economic structure of the country, to bonus others who are engaged in a business which everybody knows to be more profitable than farming on the plains. The Government knows the facts as well as we do, and I think there is nothing to add to what has been already been said.
